Jean Rees

Winterbourne House, 53-55 Argyle Road, Reading RG1 7YL
[email: Rexhaigh@winterbourne.demon.co.uk]

Jean Rees  

Development of psychodynamic psychotherapy services has not been a priority in recent years, and existing services have a responsibility to provide impetus for growth and development of provision across the country. Southern Counties Psychotherapy is a federation of psychodynamic psychotherapy services providing a Clinical Training in Psychodynamic Psychotherapy within the NHS, linked to an M.Sc. in Psychodynamic Psychotherapy in Health Service Settings. This is a rigorous analytic training, to the standards of the UKCP PPP Section, specifically addressing realities of practice within the NHS and the relationship to broader mental health services. The core philosophy is that good quality psychodynamic psychotherapies can only be available for populations if good quality psychodynamic psychotherapy training is also readily available.

We offer this description of the course and its background as encouragement for others who may want to set up similar projects, and to invite collaborators.

Elements of the Oedipus Complex: Building up the Picture

Richard Rusbridger

Richard Rusbridger

27 Normanby Road, London NW 10 1BU. e-mail: r@rusbridger.demon.co.uk

Richard Rusbridger  

The topic of the conference is how central we see the Oedipus complex as being in analysis and therefore, by implication, in the mind. I will be suggesting that the psychoanalytic theory of the Oedipal situation describes a fundamental dynamic of the mind, which in turn structures the mind. This turns on the subject's response to witnessing a creative relationship of which he is the product and from which he is excluded. This structure and dynamic operate in the mind on all levels of scale, both intrapyschically and interpsychically. They function on every level of psychosexual development and determine the form that this development takes. This centrality means that analysing the patient's characteristic reactions to the Oedipus complex is the core task of analysis. I argue that these reactions can be seen most clearly in the patient's response to the work of analysis.

If, however, the Oedipus complex is as basic and important as this, why is it sometimes thought not to be? I shall make some suggestions as to why this might be so. In particular I comment on how defensive and attacking processes often - perhaps even usually - obscure the open manifestation of an Oedipal situation in analysis. This means that what one sees is not a whole picture but fragments or elements of one. I suggest that the emergence of meaning in analysis is a key Oedipal moment, both for the analyst and the patient, and as such is attacked quite generally. The Oedipal situation in analysis does not consist in only those moments when patterns are evident that one would call ‘Oedipal’, but in this whole process of engendering, disguising, attacking and tolerating meaning.

Freud said that what he came to call in 1910 ‘the Oedipus complex’ (Freud 1910) was central to psychological development and he called it ‘the nuclear complex [Kerncomplex] of the neuroses’ (Freud 1909b). His account of the Oedipus complex was of a relationship between whole objects: love, largely unconscious, for the parent of the opposite sex was accompanied by sexual possessiveness and by a wish to eliminate the parent of the same sex. The child's intense love was accompanied by murderous hatred, and this love and hate were divided between the parents. Freud implied, though did not emphasize, the child's hatred of being the one excluded from the parents' relationship; and he did not write about the child's envy of the parents' relationship.

The Therapist as Outsider: The Truth of the Stranger

Sherly Williams

Sherly Williams

31 Kingsway Road, Leicester LE5 5TN

Sherly Williams  

This paper considers the surprising fact that, despite all we know of how ‘otherness’ causes psychic retreats of various kinds, therapy provides a remarkable instance of ‘other-ness’ being sought out. The patient in distress turns not to a familiar and trusted figure but to an outsider, a stranger. The unique nature of the therapist's perspective from this outsider's vertex is here explored within the context of current analytic debate about objectivity, subjectivity and intersubjectivity, and in the light of analytic tradition as well as historical and cultural antecedents. The aim is to illustrate how the exploration of personal truth is made possible by the therapist's willingness to locate, occupy thoughtfully, and suffer the position of ‘outsider’ in relation to the patient.

Brian Martindale

Brian Martindale

Brian Martindale  

In the opening words of his foreword Stephen Fleck, Emeritus Professor of Psychiatry at Yale University, considers that this book ‘…may be the most comprehensive treatise on schizophrenia… since [that of] Manfred Bleuler’ [published in 1972].

232

As the reviewer of the book, I therefore have the challenge of making a judgement as to whether it merits this acclaim and of clarifying whether it is an important enough book for readers of this psychotherapy journal.

The book's greatest value is in its description and illustrations of a particular model of therapy and care for those who are vulnerable to schizophrenia. This has been developed in Finland and is radically different in its conceptualization and practice from that which we usually witness. In Britain, treatment for schizophrenia can be generally characterized as based on a biologically-orientated model. Treatment is centred on ‘compliance’ with long-term ‘anti-psychotic’ medication together with support services for the individual and family of very varying degrees of availability and sophistication. I wish to stress that even proven psychological approaches with very limited goals remain rarely implemented in the UK. I am thinking, for example, of the well-respected and replicated research work of Leff who has convincingly shown that specific interventions significantly reduce relapse rates in families with high levels of ‘expressed emotion’ and/or excessive hours of contact between sufferer and family (Leff et al. 1990). This research was actually carried out in Britain and the evidence dates back 20 years. Likewise psychodynamic understandings are now rarely utilized in individual, group or family approaches although cognitive therapy has attracted some attention in very recent years. I shall return to this observation on the lack of implementation of even evidence-based psychological findings at the end of my review.

Lawrence Welch

Lawrence Welch

Lawrence Welch  

It was with some excitement that I flicked through the pages of this book addressing the complex and contentious area of remembering childhood sexual abuse, as it unexpectedly also covered issues and authors of special interest to me: the relationship between the social and the personal; the concept of intersubjectivity; Marx and Hegel.

Prager seeks to bridge the chasm between psychology and sociology by giving an account of his analysis of Ms A. The youngest in a large working-class fundamentalist Christian family, she had a special relationship with her mother, a controlling, demanding woman. Her father, the subject of criticism in the family for his alcoholism, was withdrawn but at times verbally abusive. Key events in her childhood were the death of her grandmother when she was 2 and the death of an aunt when 7.

Ms A's mother died in the first year of the analysis and shortly afterwards she began to suspect she had been sexually abused by her father. Prager was struck by the contrast between the lucidity of Ms A's previously reported childhood memories and the relative vagueness and paucity of her description of sexual abuse.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis80, 465, 1999

The Narcissistic Scenarios of Parenthood

J. Manzano, F. Palacio Espasa and N. Zilkha

The authors begin by pointing out that Freud always considered parent-child relations in terms of the child's psychic development and took little account of the parents' experience of the relationship and its psychic effects on them. They recall Freud's distinction between the anaclitic and narcissistic modes of relationship and show how these are unconsciously embodied and enacted in varying proportions in the cases observed in their own clinical practice of therapeutic consultations with parents and young children. After a review of the relevant psychoanalytic literature, the authors present their concept of the narcissistic scenarios of parenthood, which include parental projection on to the child, parental counter-identification, a specific aim and a relational dynamic that is acted out. Depending on the individual situation, the effects may help to structure the developing psyche or, if the narcissistic element is excessive, they may be pathological. The authors consider the literature on the application of psychoanalysis to therapeutic interventions with parents and children, stressing the technical importance of establishing a therapeutic focus. These ideas are illustrated by a detailed case history showing the interaction between a mother and a 4-year-old girl and how it was modified by a short therapy. The differences between interpretation in this situation and in the classical psychoanalytic setting are explained, and the paper ends with some comments on the transmission of psychic elements from generation to generation.



International Journal Of Psycho-Analysis80, 477, 1999

Some Functions of being Fair and Just - or Not - in Clinical Psychoanalysis

Eric Rayner

The author suggests that the concepts of fairness and justice might be psychoanalytically useful. They are social ideas but often arise clinically. Since psychoanalysis is about intimate and internal events, the wide social and legal settings associated with formal justice are not addressed. Fairness and informal justice arise more intimately and are central here. Fairness is concerned with thorough consideration of an issue. To be fair, the people involved must be considered with impartiality before a decision. Justice generally is more formal, aiming to ensure the integrity of a system, its parts and individual members. It is noted that psychopathogenic conditions can arise in conflicting situations involving fairness and justice. Clinical illustrations suggest that the psychoanalytic process can implicitly aim to resolve their after-effects. Technique is addressed in this light. A central suggestion emerges here. The philosopher Jurgen Habermas proposes that justice rests essentially upon opportunity for argumentation between all those affected. The author suggests that psychoanalytic therapy is likewise a constructive argumentation.

Introduction

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

The idea of having a section in this issue and the next, entitled ‘Australia: Clinical and Cross-Cultural Perspectives’ came out of discussions that Ann Scott and I had about our experiences of separately visiting Australia in 1998. Our visits had had a powerful impact upon us, and we both wanted to make more widely known a little of what we encountered. In the next issue, Ann Scott will continue the Australian section with material being developed from work presented at a conference on ‘Trauma and Memory: Cross-Cultural Perspectives’ in Sydney in May 1998.

In this issue there are two papers, one that looks back and gives a vivid and personal account about psychoanalysis in the 1950s in Australia. And the other paper is about original work that is currently being done with mothers and children in Melbourne. I felt there was something we could learn from the past and present Australian experience of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis. We all have a tendency to believe that our own institutional practices embody ‘wisdom’ and ‘truth’, and psychotherapy seems particularly vulnerable to this weakness. It was therefore very invigorating to be reminded that psychotherapeutic teaching and practice can change and adapt. It is a cliche to speak of the vast spaces between the cities in Australia, but there was something refreshingly original in the way in which the Australian Psychotherapy Trainings and Services have been forced to think about the resources that are to hand. For instance, if the therapist that you want to supervise your work lives 3000 miles away, you set up telephone supervision. But it is not only trainings that have adapted to the environment, but the therapeutic work has stretched into the communities in interesting ways. The first paper, ‘Synergy of Verbal and Non-verbal Therapies in the Treatment of Mother-Infant Relationships’ by Helga Coulter and Elizabeth Loughlin, working in Melbourne, is a challenging account of the combination of dance therapy and psychoanalytic therapy for disturbed and depressed mothers and infants. What makes this work particularly pertinent to today's climate, whether in Australia or elsewhere, is that their intervention is short term. In a very different vein we publish ‘A Memoir of My Psychoanalysis with Dr Clara Geroe’ by Deirdre Moore. This paper has already been published in the Australian Journal of Psychotherapy (1999) 17 (1 & 2), but I wanted it reproduced here for it most beautifully recaptures the last and precious moments of a central European psychoanalytic culture that was still recognizably itself while adapting itself to its enforced exile.

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone

London

Jennifer Silverstone  

This book, by definition, is a book to be read. The reading of it creates a particular demand on the reader, a demand that cannot necessarily be met. The book takes us back in time into the fragments of childhood memories that the adult author had held in his mind, and that he has shaped and woven into consciousness. His narrative begins with the terror of his family's physical disintegration and the death of what we take to be his father, when he was a very young child. The story develops with the reader's dawning awareness that these episodes of childhood have been spent within concentration camps. The author has survived fearful experiences and been liberated from the camps and has eventually been adopted by a family who denies his past. The denial is total. There is no space made for the working through of the trauma of his previous existence so he struggles to discover the truth of his past and the history that shaped it.

There is specificity about his past, as we would expect. It is his story, and history. It has integrity, and we the readers are asked to believe it. It has an honesty which transcends judgement and criticism. This seems to be because he says the unsayable and leaves the reader with the unthinkable. There is no analysis here and no judgement. These are the truths of the human heart. They have to be truths because our imagination falls short of the reality of the moral disorder that he offers us.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis79, 1071, 1998

Psychoanalysis and Cognitive-Evolutionary Psychology: An Attempt at Integration

Paolo Migone and Giovanni Liotti

The authors argue that the abandonment of the theory of trauma in 1897 was a trauma for Freud himself who was led to ‘despair’ and possibly reacted with an overemphasis on inner fantasies and drive discharge. They suggest that today we are facing a second trauma in the history of psychoanalysis that we might call the ‘abandonment of drive theory’, i.e. the notion that human beings strive not primarily to reduce sexual and aggressive drives but rather seek objects, assign meanings, test previous beliefs and assimilate new schemes. Our task is to recover as Freud was able to do, giving a new impetus to psychoanalysis. The current challenge is, on the one hand, a revision of the psychoanalytic conception of inherited information and, on the other, a theory of motivation based on converging evidence from cognitive science, ethology, infant research and psychotherapy research. Many clinical models are current in contemporary psychoanalysis. Only as one example among these models, some concepts used in Weiss and Sampson's Control Mastery Theory will be discussed in the light of cognitive science and evolutionary epistemology within the framework of (a) the 1960 classic, Plans and Structure of Behavior by Miller, Galanter and Pribram, (b) Edelman's neurobiological theory and (c) Bowlby's attachment theory.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis79, 1115, 1998

‘Black Holes’, Deadness and Existing Analytically

Ofra Eshel

In this paper, the author makes metaphorical use of the astrophysical term ‘black hole’ to describe the impact of the psychically ‘dead’ mother. The ‘dead’ mother constitutes a ‘black hole’ experience in the interpersonal, intersubjective space of her child because of the intense grip and compelling pull of her world of inner deadness. Individuals under her influence are either trapped in her deadening world or, if they succeed in detaching themselves, are petrified in their interpersonal space, because of the imminent threat of being drawn back in again. Consequently, they are unable to form object relations of closeness, love and intimate bonding. Can analysis provide the enormous counter-forces needed for freeing them from the grip of these powerful, devouring forces? The author describes the analysis of a man who grew up with a ‘dead’ mother. Analysis began with a patient who was emotionally disconnected. developed into patient (and analyst) being drawn into a ‘black hole’ of deadness and dying, and eventually progressed to his extrication. The emphasis here is on the analytic experience and analytic experiencing. The author relates experientially and theoretically to the pivotal role of the patientanalyst's survival of the deadening, destructive processes in this analysis, and the analyst's capacity (and struggle) to both hold and contain the patient, and remain alive, while experiencing and going through annihilation and death along with the patient.

Putting the Record Straight

Jan Birtle

Jan Birtle

Birmingham

Jan Birtle  

Dear Editor

I was very surprised to read a letter in your Journal from John Rowan (1998), commenting on a paper published by two of my former trainees (Paul & Bluck 1997), which appears to have been printed with no opportunity for commentary from the authors.

I was also very concerned to see that John Rowan did not appear to have read, or at least understood, the article in terms of what it was attempting to convey. As the coordinator of the scheme in which these trainees participated, I think it is important that we get the chance to put the record straight. The scheme was initiated under the guidance of The Royal College of Psychiatrists in order that psychiatric trainees are all given the opportunity to participate in clinical practice which is supervised by a psychotherapist. There was no suggestion in the article that graduates from this scheme would then be skilled psychodynamic psychotherapists; however, some of the trainees may go on to apply for specialist psychotherapeutic training after participation in this scheme.

I would be very interested to hear John Rowan's early experiences in psychotherapy. Is he suggesting that anyone interested in working clinically with patients should have extensive, personal analysis prior to this? If so, perhaps he should make his views known to The Royal College of Psychiatrists. Certainly that would mean that Mental Health Services outside London would completely grind to a halt, as there is not sufficient psychoanalytic resource available in the provinces to provide for the vast number of trainees who would be affected.

My final point is perhaps one of greatest concern. John Rowan states: ‘I seriously wonder if the Uffculme Clinic has not gone collectively mad’. The Uffculme Clinic is a well-established NHS psychotherapy centre which provides a regional service for people residing in the West Midlands.

While I would be very happy for John Rowan to write direct to members of the Clinic to mention his concerns that we may have gone ‘collectively mad’, I find it less than satisfactory that such a statement appears in a publicly-available journal, with no opportunity for the simultaneous publication of a response. Clearly, for the five million population we serve, such a statement could engender tremendous anxieties and concerns about the mental health and well-being of the therapists providing this treatment. To put the record straight, I would like to reassure John Rowan, and readers of your Journal, that the Uffculme Psychotherapy Service, as it is now known, provides a clinical service that is well underpinned by staff training, skills development and clinical supervision.

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers  

The Christian millennium approaches, with millennialist phenomena - the ‘Cult of the Sun’ arrange mass suicides in Switzerland and Tenerife. According to American clinical psychologist Richard Noll's best-seller The Jung Cult (1994), C.G. Jung counts with them: an extreme right-winger, begetter of a personality cult - The Arian Christ (Noll 1996); hence the Cult Fictions of the title of the book under review.

525

Noll's thesis received much academic acclaim. If true, analytical psychology is not therapy, but rather a cabal of greedy charlatans engaged in ‘one of the most successful examples of pyramid selling in human history’. This is a serious charge with highly damaging consequences for patients and professionals alike.

Sonu Shamdasani, Historian of Psychology at the Wellcome Institute, London, inadvertently provided fuel for Noll's fire. In his book, Appendix Three, ‘Of Scholarship’, recounts a tangled web of intellectual skulduggery surrounding a tattered piece of paper at the centre of the debate. Labelled ‘Analytical collectivity’, the document was found amongst papers belonging to Fanny Bowdich Katz, a young American whose father was a close friend of William James. Suffering from depression, she was sent to Zurich, saw Jung, and analysed with Maria Moltzer, one of his early assistants.

Noll takes the document as Jung's founding address to the Analytical Psychology Club, Zurich. His book gives a ‘fly on the wall’ account of its reverential reception at the Club's first meeting. Unfortunately, Shamdasani suggests, this never happened. The ‘Inaugural Minutes’, reproduced here, are a prosaic procedural record, in tone more Women's Institute than Satanist ring.

Shamdasani reveals in this book his claim that ‘Analytical collectivity’ is by Moltzer. He cites the original catalogue record and provides detailed textual support, presenting it as an unpublished sketch for a paper on the transcendent function, the relationship between individual and collective, mundane and spiritual. Moltzer's views differ markedly from Jung's - expressed in his 1916 essay ‘The Transcendent Function’ (Collected Works 8, para 131-193). Moltzer related her paper to the continuing disputes in and around the Analytical Psychology Club about its purpose and function.

Val Richards  

These memorial essays in tribute to Frances Tustin display a depth and meticulousness of discussion, with illuminating clinical examples, enriched by apt

531

literary allusions (e.g. Rhode, p. 41). Fresh light is shed on ways of responding to unbearable silences and despair (Riley, p. 77; Wittenberg, p. 125). And, far from encapsulation in a private psychoanalytic world, the papers are set in a clear philosophical, existential context where the centrality of thought and language in the formation of identity is affirmed (e.g. Houzel, p. 341). The essays are therefore essential reading not only for those working with designated autistic people, but for any analytical psychotherapist likely to encounter autistic traces in ‘ordinary’ patients. In these studies of autistic states, there emerges a vision of disturbed early development which, according to most of the writers, interferes with progression towards the capacity for feeling, phantasy, projection and symbol formation. It is as if their own intimate knowledge of isolation, of desolation, of terror of both being and non-being allows the authors to confer a poetic intensity and immediacy upon scenes of inner devastation. Paradoxically, the imagery invoked to chart the enclosed and wordless world of autism has a repeatedly cosmic resonance:

It might be said that Tustin's theories speak to the origins of semiotic processes and the relationship to the ‘black hole’ which she defines as a gap or hole in the fabric of one's being. (Introduction, p. xxvii)

Notwithstanding their range and breadth, the papers are impressively cohesive and free of needless repetition. This is because Tustin's ideas (supported, in particular, by the thinking of Winnicott) irradiate the thought and practice of each contributor, with both an expansion of and a divergence from certain of her key postulates. An important unifying theme is the consensus that Tustin eventually modified her earlier belief in a primary autistic stage in normal development (pp. 5-6). The healthy infant is object-relating from the start, as confirmed by the researches of Stern, Trevarthen, et al.

A Response to ‘Discretion as Power: In the Situation Called “Psychotherapy”’ by Thomas Szasz

Peter Lomas

Peter Lomas

41 Beaulands Close, Cambridge CB4 1JA

Peter Lomas  

No one, not even R.D. Laing, has sought to defend the freedom of disturbed people from inappropriate coercion with more rigour, tenacity and courage than has Thomas Szasz (1998). He has been heavily criticized, even vilified, for his pains but remains undaunted and, as the present paper testifies, is as sharp and trenchant as ever. Szasz's quest has the force of a mission and at times leads him into writing with intemperance, but I believe that his mission is justified and that we have reasons to be grateful for his voice.

In ‘Discretion as Power’ Szasz reiterates his basic philosophical stance in relation to psychotherapy. Psychotherapy, he maintains, is only morally acceptable if the patient's freedom of action is sacrosanct. There must be no coercion either by the therapist or by a third party who has the power to influence the procedure. His focus is less upon the unjustifiable moral and intellectual pressure of the practitioner's interpretations and injunctions than on the legal and financial restraints that can be imposed on the endeavour.

Szasz's thesis that coercion is never justified in any circumstances is difficult to sustain. A less extreme version of this - and one that, I believe, Szasz can easily defend - is that the degree of coercion by the state, the agencies of the state, and the contemporary dominance of the scientific idiom is harmful, immoral and unacceptable. In spelling out the ways in which this occurs - and providing us with actual examples - Szasz unveils the sloppy thinking and hypocrisy that allows much of the phenomena to pass unnoticed.

At times Szasz appears to underestimate the resilience of therapist and patient. For example, he writes ‘It is difficult for me to conceive of “good” psychotherapy - the patient willing and eager to embrace courage, integrity and responsibility - without the client paying for the service he receives-:’ There are very few situations in life, including psychotherapy, in which a project can be undertaken in ideal conditions. Not only the matter of who pays, but many other factors can place unwelcome pressure on the integrity of the two people. But they have to make the best of it, and often do so.

Clinical Commentary XXIV

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold  

The material for this set of commentaries is the assessment sessions of a little girl being brought to the therapist by her parents. In great contrast to some of the recent presentations of work with adults there is no history or background presented. It is possible to see the interest of work with children in providing a chance to examine pure process, to look immediately at the transference and the unfolding of this new relationship.

For all the authors there are different questions raised by and framed within their different theoretical frames, but there are also convergences which make the work described recognizably therapeutic - as we see the child being helped to start to think in new ways, and psychoanalytic - with every commentator and the original therapist assuming they need to pay attention to the relationship formed between the patient and the therapist. The variations come in areas such as the use made of the transference. How explicitly and how quickly the different therapists wish to comment upon it, for instance. The question of how far differences between different schools represent some real cleavage in ways of thinking, or how far these are individual emphases, is one to ponder.

Therapy Across Culture by Inga-Britt Krause. Published by Sage, London, 1998; 193 pages; £13.99

Herbert Hahn

Herbert Hahn

Herbert Hahn  

This is an important book which has a broader relevance to psychotherapists than its title suggests. In an academically rigorous style (the bibliography itself runs to 13 pages), and drawing on her own experience as an anthropologist and systemic (family) therapist, Inga-Britt Krause shows how ethnographic methodology (fieldwork) and its research findings can be drawn on to radically deepen our clinical insight into ‘difference’. While anthropologists now largely accept that there is a universal dimension to unconscious oedipal conflict, they also assert that there are culturally distinctive paths towards its resolution. For example, in Hindu culture, where the resolution of the Oedipus complex involves an internal identification with the group rather than with the parent, submission to rather than overthrow of paternal authority is a sign of masculinity.

Krause suggests that meanings have to do with representation. Language provides for, but does not encompass the complexity of cognitive and emotional processes and their dynamic expression. As therapists we need to gain ‘background understanding’ of the ‘ethos’ or ‘habitus’ of our patients. This takes us into the realm of culture ‘as related to emotions, kinship relations, ritual and taboo (which) are located on the boundary between the internal life of an individual and the external world of relationships, customs and institutions’ (p. 140).

In Euro-American countries power lies with the white therapist trained in the disciplines and theories dominated by Euro-American philosophy. As meaning is heterodox, ‘it is always possible that the most powerful will persuade, command or even terrorize the less powerful’ (p. 153).

As therapists we need to be curious

about the social relationships, the institutions, the professional theories, the professional organizations and the history of the society or societies which have provided the background and context for our own personal and professional life and experiences (p. 167).

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The concepts handed down from our psychoanalytic forefathers, so incredibly enriching to our understanding of the human mind, nevertheless need periodic review. The Journal co-sponsors a day conference with the Freud Museum on 31 October 1998, with the title ‘Analysing the Oedipus Complex: Why It Is Still Central’. More than 200 participants attended the Institut Français in London to hear presentations on current views of the Oedipus concept. We are delighted to be able to publish the papers in this issue. In a theoretical paper, Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel writes of the structuring power of the Oedipus complex, without which desire goes unchannelled with strange results: untamed sexuality, narcissism and omnipotence, or the ‘oceanic feeling’ outside of external reality that characterizes some modern spiritual movements. Further, she goes on to discuss the way that some intersubjective analytic groups in America lack firm oedipal structuring to their disadvantage. Then, in three clinical papers, we have detailed examples of current work with patients. In the first, Julia Fabricius links the Oedipus complex to separation-individuation, mourning, and the necessity in psychic development for there to be an acknowledgement of an object separate and independent from the self, capable of having a relationship with a third object. Her patient could not relinquish his infantile dependence, both fearing and wanting the consuming mother, and lacking an internal father. Richard Rusbridger and Gigliola Fornari Spoto both use the Kleinian framework in which it is believed the outcome of oedipal love has vital implications for the urge to learn, the ‘epistemophilic impulse’, and for the acceptance of and relationship to reality. Tolerating the deprivations involved in giving up possession of parents goes together with tolerating depressive affect, loss and separation and acceptance of the world outside the self. Giving up oedipal yearnings enables a structuring of the internal world, the internalization of a creative parental couple separate from the self. Psychic space structured in such a way has been termed by Britton (1998) ‘triangular space’, an aspect from which the self can witness a relationship of which one is not a part, a third position of observing and being seen that mitigates envy and jealousy and creates space for individual thinking. Richard Rusbridger's paper links the oedipal situation with the depressive position and the emergence of meaning. Rusbridger develops the idea that the patient's stance in the oedipal relationship is closely related to the process of engendering, disguising, attacking or valuing meaning, the fate of the mating of ideas between therapist and patient. Rusbridger's case material is from the analyses of a child, a borderline and a neurotic. Gigliola Fornari Spoto's paper stresses the choice between self'-knowledge and self-deception, fundamental to every therapeutic journey and hinging on the acceptance or rejection of oedipal truth.

Helen Robinson

Helen Robinson

London

Helen Robinson  

As the condensation of meaning in the single title word of this anthology of poetry testifies, Generations is poetic man's and, in preponderance, twentieth century poetic man's concentration upon connectedness, the narrow vein of meaning that shapes us, that is, our ‘generation’ from one another, and how we come, in the fine detail of poetry, to experience it. It is also the poetry written by one generation to another. It is of and by generations, and produces ‘generations’, that is, poems.

The result is a new form, as the editors suggest in their fine introduction, ‘the huge increase in the volume of work (this century) which speaks directly of parent or child’ (p. xiii), a new seed or seeds that can now grow from such generation, and the editors speak of this, their creation, their anthology of this particular parent and child verse, as ‘almost like witnessing the birth of a new poetic genre’ (p. xiii).

In one way, it may be described as a distortion of these individual poets and their breadth of output to select the ‘generational’ themes of their poetic discourse. And yet in another way, in my view, a more profound way, it is a celebration of a particular truth about creativity and generation. It is a wonderful point of reference. For all creators, conceivers, generators derive from and out of that which lies most intimately and, paradoxically, most unknowingly beside them. That human intercourse at its height, enabled by the intimacy and closeness offered by birth, living alongside death, that with which we are most ‘familiar’, that this can be the source of poetry, the subject of creativity, for me indicates the paradox of estrangement and distance and exclusion that lies at the heart of all that connects us.

If when we are at our closest we are also, simultaneously, at our furthest point, one from the other as, inevitably, poets, by choosing to write of and out of their own love and ‘at handedness’ suggest, then do our great artists thus plead on our behalf for closure of this vastness, this immeasurable unknowable gap?

For and Against Psychoanalysis by Stephen Frosh. Published by Routledge, London, 1997; 271 pages; £12.99

Jean White

Jean White

Jean White  

In For and Against Psychoanalysis, Stephen Frosh locates contemporary psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic theory within epistemological, therapeutic and socio-political contexts. In so doing, he aims to examine its efficacy as a means of learning, a clinical method and a theoretical instrument - this latter with particular

529

reference to the deconstruction and understanding of gender identity, sexuality and racism. He expounds a critical view of psychoanalysis, particularly in relation to its potentially normalizing tendencies, but also in terms of its lack of accountability and relative failure (at least as measured by research so far) as a clinical treatment. He also uses psychoanalysis as a perspective from which to scrutinize Western empiricism and positivism - the limits and limitations of the ‘rational’ as thrown into high relief by the ‘science’ of the irrational. This is essentially a theoretical work that can probably be of equal value within academic and psychotherapeutic contexts.

For and Against Psychoanalysis is clearly written but never simplistic. Frosh's theoretical standpoints absolutely belie the stark polarizations implicit in the title. He is master of the third unexpected twist of the dialectic to complicate, sophisticate and surprise, in a way not unlike the workings of the unconscious itself. For example, in the first section on ‘Knowledge’, at times he appears to be propounding a sceptical view of psychoanalysis as a research instrument (too subjective, too variable, too deeply interpersonal, too ‘slippery’). Nonetheless, his final conclusions - that ‘real knowledge involves emotion at its core’ and that ‘…there is no ‘unbiased’ part of the mind which could be called upon to act as neutral observer of events’ (p. 71) - serve notice on the value of empirical rationality as the basis of research in the human sciences.

Similarly, in the central section on ‘Psychotherapy’, the logic of his style and cool clarity of his arguments are belied by his penchant for the subversive and disruptive as preferred theoretical resting points.

Commentary by a Jungian Child Analyst

Susan Rees

Susan Rees

An Skyber, Trevithal, Near Paul, Penzance

Susan Rees  

Session 1

Natalie seems uncertain where her place is in the room and she is relieved when the therapist offers her the chair. Is this her experience in her family - unsure where she fits, in relation to the others? I was struck with the absence of others in the drawing of the girl having her lunch alone, and I wondered what the tracksuit meant for her (a warm covering garment or a garment in which you compete on racing tracks?)

She tells the therapist that she cries and her tummy aches and she does not want to go to the language classes: ‘they (the parents) pull me and I don't want to move and they can't’.

Is she telling the therapist something about her difficulty in separation, which her parents ‘can't’ help her with? I wondered also from these remarks what the birth experience had been like. Does her remark also indicate her anger/resistance to being moved out and on into language classes and growing up?

Her sobbing seemed to be triggered off by looking into the box and the dolls-house and I wondered if these stood for the insides of mother's body where the babies/ siblings are lodged, i.e. the loss of her infant experience and needs which perhaps were not fully met. The parents' view of her ‘attention-seeking’ behaviour imply a difficulty in thinking about her emotional needs and the more infantile aspects of her personality. My view may be substantiated by the persona of the tracksuited girl and her disregard for the ‘babyish’ toys in Session 2, so she might at this tearful stage be struggling with a phase of the depressive position.

She did respond well to the therapist and could take what was offered, so that her perception of the therapist was not one of a persecuting object.

Session 2

Is it harder to leave mother when her younger brother is there and she cries as she leaves her, and does her depression make her ‘not care’ when the therapist asks her where she wants to sit, though she chooses again the small chair: an indication that this is a place where her infant self can be tolerated? I wondered whether the therapist's comment about the tissue being a help made her able to make links in her subsequent drawing: do the two shapes stand for the links the therapist makes for her, between her head - the thinking top square, and her body - the tummy ache and somatic bottom square? Perhaps they stand for the therapist and herself.

Introductory Comments from the Chairman

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

This is the sixth conference held jointly by the British Journal of Psychotherapy and the Freud Museum and the collaboration between our two organizations has been highly beneficial all around. Not only does it provide worthwhile conference events for the public, but the proceeds of this conference will go to the Freud Museum to help support their programmes, and the BJP has the opportunity to publish the fine papers that have been prepared for the Conference. I'd like to thank Erica Davies, the curator, Ivan Ward, the Education Officer, and all the staff, for the work that has made the Conference possible.

To introduce our topic. Much of the groundwork on Freud's monumental book The Interpretation of Dreams was completed before 1896; however its publication in 1900 would have to await Freud's own self-analysis, the analysis of his dreams, and the further thinking that led to his discovery of the Oedipus complex. Adopting the myth of Oedipus Rex, Freud introduced his new idea in The Interpretation of Dreams, saying:

The destiny of King Oedipus moves us only because it might have been ours - because the oracle laid the same curse upon us before our birth as upon him. It is the fate of all of us, perhaps, to direct our first sexual impulse towards our mother and our first hatred and our first murderous wish against our father. Our dreams convince us that that is so. King Oedipus, who slew his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta, merely shows us the fulfilment of our own childhood wishes. (1900, pp. 262-3)

Freud goes on to give the Oedipus concept a central position in his writing. In developing the theory of infant sexuality that he presented in the Three Essays in 1905, Freud states that it is the ‘nuclear complex’ of all the neuroses, emphasizing its universality unequivocally when he says, ‘Every new arrival on this planet is faced by the task of mastering the Oedipus Complex’. Freud's first published study involving the oedipal dilemma was in 1908 with his description of Little Hans. Then in 1910 in his paper on ‘The Psychology Of Love’ he wrote of children's phantasies of parental intercourse, with accompanying affects of jealousy and revenge. By the time he wrote his account of the Wolf Man in 1918, the witnessing of the primal scene was viewed as the core of his patient's illness, and he went on to elaborate in his later texts the oedipal as a psychosexual phase in his developmental scheme.

Conundrums of Gender and ‘Amikam’

Lawrence Suss

Lawrence Suss

Brighton

Lawrence Suss  

Dear Editor

I wonder if you are able to shed some light on a conundrum that emerged in a group I teach at the University.

We were discussing a paper from Vol. 9(4) of the BJP, ‘Suicidal Acts Among Latency-Age Children as an Expression of Internal Object-Relations’ by Dr Yecheskiel Cohen. One of the students is Israeli and drew my attention to two anomalies:

The footnote to the paper on page 405 provides details of Dr Cohen's employment and refers to Dr Cohen as a ‘she’. Yecheskiel is apparently a man's name.

Of more importance, and of some impact on the argument in the paper, Dr Cohen translates the name of one of her/his patients incorrectly. On page 406 ‘Amikam’ is translated as ‘my father has arisen’ whereas it actually means ‘my people have arisen’. To be ‘my father has arisen’ the name would have to be ‘Avikam’ - close, but not the same.

I wonder if anyone else has written to you raising these points (I recognize that the paper is now six years old and you were not the Editor then), and what the outcome was.

Yours sincerely Lawrence Suss

University of Sussex, Brighton

Jean Arundale replies:

Thank you for your comments relating to the article by Dr Yecheskiel Cohen in BJP 9(4). No one, including the author, has written to correct us on the two points you make, so they remain conundrums.

Blind Alleys: Obstacles Along the Road to Intimacy by Gerald Alper. Published by International Scholars Publications, San Francisco, London, Bethesda, 1998; 157 pages; $34.95 hardback, also available in paperback

Viveka Nyberg

Viveka Nyberg

London

Viveka Nyberg  

This is the sixth book in five years from this prolific American author. Gerald Alper was a novelist and short story writer who trained as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist. Blind Alleys is presented as the continuation of his first book as a psychotherapist: The Singles Scene - A Psychoanalytical Study of the Breakdown of Intimacy (1994). In The Singles Scene Alper came to the conclusion that there has been a systematic and unconscious erosion of what is generally meant by intimacy. The blind alleys referred to in the title are, according to the author; ‘relational deadends, standoffs and tradeoffs’ (pp. iv). Throughout the book Alper refers to ‘intimacy -hunger’ and ‘intimacy panic’ as the two factors which encourage blind alleys. It is the individual resolution of the tension between these two urges of need and fear which determines whether someone finds themself in a ‘blind alley’ which preserves the status quo or, alternatively, is able to find a more creative solution. Alper stresses that he does not simply see blind alleys as dysfunctional defences but that he regards them as serving the protective and dynamic function of foreclosing the prospects of the terrors of intimacy. Alper refers throughout the book to the theories of Freud, Bollas and Winnicott. He sees himself as a psychoanalytical psychotherapist in the objectrelations tradition. However he also incorporates a wider social view of the difficulties of achieving intimacy and how these difficulties are played out within the arena of society.

It is not entirely clear towards whom the book is primarily targeted. On the face of it the book is addressed to a general reader. It is full of popular colloquialisms and the language is lively and informal. On the other hand it also addresses complex theoretical concepts which perhaps are better understood by the professional reader. Moreover, the author's unwieldy sentences may present a challenge to any reader.

The book is divided into three parts. The first part is presented as a catalogue of different forms of blind alleys. The chapters have titles like: ‘The Blackmailer’, ‘The Screamer’, ‘The Narcissistic Great Man’, etc. The titles refer to the diversity of different kinds of blind alleys which Alper perceives as self-contained psychic states from which intimacy has been barred. In the chapter ‘Worrying About the Other’, Alper describes his work with a patient who consistently brought into the sessions her obsessive concerns with her grown-up daughter. What is missing in Alper's exploration of worrying as a clinical manifestation is the acknowledgement of the patient's internal object. In other words, what part of the patient does the daughter represent? There are instances in the book where it would arguably be appropriate to interject the missing internal object. In the context of the obsessively worrying patient Alper also seems to omit the possibility that excessive worrying may be understood as an indication of the ambivalent nature of the relationship.

Silvia Goldie

Silvia Goldie

40 Parkhill Road, London NW3 2YB

Silvia Goldie  

This clinical material belongs to the initial stages of the psychotherapy treatment of a 7-year-old girl. All we know about her is her age, the fact that she is the third of four children, and a reference made by herself about inconsolable crying, abdominal pains and the refusal to attend some classes.

Natalie seemed to come into the consulting room easily. She is described as a slight child', which probably refers to her build, but maybe also about a way to enter situations trying not to take too much space. Hesitant when she comes in, she appears to the psychotherapist to be relieved when she is invited to sit down on a child's chair. It brings to mind that, for Natalie, there is a relief in being allowed to be a child; not to have to take care of anybody or make decisions herself. In her drawing the frame seems to be important. I thought that the picture expressed her need to have a context within which she could be a child that could nourish and grow into a chair that is too big at the moment. It may be a reference to something in herself that requires to be fed so that she can learn. Something in pain, unattended, that contributes to a level of anorexia. She is a hungry girl in a tracksuit, which hints at a certain sexual ambiguity, perhaps a desire to be a boy.

Natalie seems surprised, ‘uncertain’, when she hears the interpretation. I think that in these first moments of the session she has projected what she hopes this new relationship could provide for her - to satisfy her need of nourishment. The psychotherapist does not pause over this as long as I would have done and chooses to refer to the reason for being there, and the possible likely meaning of the abdominal pains.

The title of Margaret Arden's excellent book may be a touch misleading and disappoint those whose appetites have been whetted in anticipation of an exploration of the soul. Her book, which is a collection of papers published between 1984-1997, belongs to that current of enquiry and research that seeks to place a tradition of thought and practice in relation to contemporary and evolving paradigms. Clinical Material

Assessment of Natalie: First Session

Natalie is 7-years-old, the third of four children. She comes into the waiting room with mother with an anxious smile revealing some missing teeth. She is quite a slight child. Natalie comes into the consulting room with me and looks around uncertainly, not knowing where to sit or what to do. I offer her one of the children's chairs and she accepts with relief.

The box is open on the table, and there is some paper; Natalie takes the crayons, carefully pulling out each colour that she wants. She draws a kind of frame like the curtains for a stage. She spends quite a bit of time on this part of the drawing. She then draws a child sitting in a big chair at a table with a plate and cutlery set on it. I ask her who it is, she draws the hair and says it is a girl in a tracksuit eating lunch. I wonder if it is her, all by herself. Natalie looks at me uncertainly.

I ask her if she knows why her mother and father have brought her to see me and why they have come to talk to me about their worries about her. She says, ‘My parents can't handle me when I'm crying and my tummy aches and I don't want to go to language classes. They pull me but I don't want to move and they can't.’

I say, ‘Maybe you have cross feelings that come out as your tummy-ache, it is a way of showing that you are feeling unhappy.’ Natalie nods.

Integration of Theory

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto  

Dear Editor

I would like to offer a response to the two papers in the Winter issue (BJP 15(2), 1998) by Stephen Mitchell and Susie Orbach.

The increasing number of calls for the ‘integration’ of theories must, I think, indicate a desire both for more clarity and for less conflict between the various theoryespousing groups. I do not know how theories ‘integrate’ (and I rather suspect they don't), but it would be good if we could think more about what we are saying and see what are the overlaps, disagreements and so on. I would like to make an attempt, in the hope that I may also provoke response from readers.

Stephen Mitchell's paper is one of a number in recent years advocating the inclusion (or some similar term) of attachment theory in psychotherapeutic work, e.g. Migone and Lotti (1998). Although I work analytically, as does Stephen Mitchell, I have no problem with attachment theory, which seems to me to have illuminated human behaviour and to have established its findings by way of the careful evaluation of empirical evidence. Furthermore, its findings have, on the whole, confirmed the findings of analytic work which should be a cause for satisfaction to analytic folk. I am thinking here not only of work specifically labelled attachment theory but also of the work of experimentalists like Daniel Stern, who may not place themselves in this camp.

My question is: as an analytical practitioner, what do I do with this work? Attachment theory, being experimentally based, has an underpinning of evidence not readily available to theory derived from the consulting room. It is theory about a population and moreover a theory which is probabilistic, i.e. statistically based. It makes statements which aim to be general or universal in nature. How are these to be placed within psychoanalytic practice?

To take Mitchell's work with Connie, Connie's separation is depicted as a hole, and Mitchell devotes his efforts to understanding the nature of this hole, what is (not) in the hole, what the boundaries of the hole consist of and so forth. This seems to me to be sound psychoanalytic thinking. So how does attachment theory come in?

Belief and Imagination: Explorations in Psychoanalysis by Ronald Britton. Published in the New Library of Psychoanalysis by Routledge, London, 1998; 226 pages; £ 17.99

Brendan McLoughlin

Brendan McLoughlin

Brendan McLoughlin  

In Belief and Imagination: Explorations in Psychoanalysis, Ronald Britton presents us with an important work. He does so in a style that is admirably inclusive, avoiding those pitfalls of abstruseness and impenetrability which sometimes mar the contributions of other writers who may be affected by those very issues connected with publication anxiety that he discusses and develops so interestingly in his final chapter. His central thesis is that, alongside the love and hate instincts familiar to us, there is a separate instinct for knowledge which contributes its own complications in the development of the individual. He sees belief as a component of the instinct for knowledge, necessary to us so that we can, as he puts it, act and react in the world, often in the absence of actual knowledge. One of the conflicts the individual must face in relation to his or her beliefs is that they may collapse in the light of experience which affords knowledge. When a belief fails under the impact of reality the individual needs to mourn its loss, which may become a central task in the therapeutic relationship, taken up in the process of working through.

Britton is to be admired for the clarity with which he develops and presents his argument against the sequence of theoretical development traced from Freud through Klein, Bion, Winnicott and others. One has the sense of a writer who troubles to make plain the difficult concepts he is developing. Indeed the overall impression is of a well-crafted book, which manages to introduce a significant contribution to the psychoanalytic paradigm which is both theoretically intelligent and likely to be clinically applicable. His description of the instinct for knowledge, and his anatomizing of the components of belief and imagination are welcome presentations of concepts which the practising psychotherapist will find helpful. He methodically develops and integrates his insights within the existing psychoanalytic paradigm, especially with reference to the oedipal picture and the primal scene as discussed in his ideas about triangular space and the ‘other room’, as well as in relation to the major Kleinian concepts of the paranoid-schizoid position and the depressive position. However from almost the middle of the book to its end there is a major shift, almost one might say as if Britton vacates the consulting room to enter the other room of literature. Clearly this does fall within the aims of The New Library of Psychoanalysis, and what Britton manages to do in these chapters is both fascinating and stimulating. I very much enjoyed reading his analysis of various poets and found it, in a sense, both comforting and reassuring to discover psychoanalytic concepts and ideas so well illustrated in their vision and insight. However, I was also left wondering if I was not being seduced. This is a scholarly work, entirely impressive in its scope and depth of critical analysis. It did make me feel that I wanted to pick up Wordsworth and Rilke, Milton and Blake and that I would want to re-read Belief and Imagination itself. Clearly this is not a book to dispatch in one reading, more a text to study and digest.

The Future of Psychotherapy in the UK: Discussing Clinical Governance

Ian Owen MA UKCP

Ian Owen

Wulfruna Street, Wolverhampton, WV1 1SB. [e mail: csl869@wlv.ac.uk]

Ian Owen  

‘Clinical governance’ is a term coined to denote a requirement that all forms of clinical care should be governed by an attention to the quality of its delivery to the public. Clinical governance has been set as the future for the NHS by the NHS Executive. This paper draws together some of the themes of current discussions concerning clinical governance and other related issues for psychotherapy. Clinical governance has many facets but it can be defined as a commitment to evidence-based quality assurance in relation to clear national standards for practice, the delivery of evidence-based practice and the ongoing monitoring of standards. The paper provides a brief outline of clinical governance and indicates how it might be accomplished within primary and secondary care. A sketch is made concerning the possibility of there being local and national standards for various aspects of psychotherapy provision which is an additional requirement. The term ‘psychotherapy’ is used to cover the full range of psychological interventions. Towards the end of the paper a critical overview of the standard paradigm of quantitative research is presented. This critical stance has been provided by two leading quantitative researchers who have called into question the applicability of the drug trial model for testing efficacy and finding the change-active ingredients of psychotherapy.

The material for this commentary is a session of work in ongoing marital therapy. As always the generosity of all the contributors needs acknowledging. The task of presenting work to public scrutiny and the time and thought put into the commentaries are considerable, and it is valuable for all of us able to read the results.

The question of how we characterize the psychoanalytic endeavour is an issue the commentaries inevitably illuminate. The emphasis upon process, the interaction within the session, the interest in perception rather than external fact, and the search for knowledge, however uncomfortable that knowledge may be, come through in these contributions from different thinkers. Listening to this account I feel jarred right at the beginning. The lift. We are, it seems, in an institutional setting. The transference, or indeed the ‘pre-formed’ transference, is shaped by images of the extended family that is often sharper and more dramatic than in a private setting. Encountering ‘siblings’, for example, is more likely. We are alerted to the therapists' countertransference more by way of a flashing light than by an invitation into that experience. I register ‘this was extraordinarily perturbing’ in reference to someone else coming out of the lift before the couple. To the couple, to the therapists? We are not told, and, of course, cannot ask as one might in supervision. Perhaps it is just as well. Already I am thinking about a countertransference in which ‘self and other’ boundaries are not clearly marked. Perhaps they do not need to be because they are clearly felt. But I am wondering. ‘Shook hands with each of us.’ European? Very formal, or friendly, or needing or wanting physical contact. Very quickly we are in a world where separation and contact raise issues (but, as yet, only in my imagination). So, I wait.

Commentary by a Group Analyst and Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Anne Morgan

Anne Morgan

Mountgrove Practice, 78 Mountgrove Road, London N5 2LT

Anne Morgan   The Group Analytic Network, 132 Stapleton Hall Road, London N4 4QB Member of the Institute of Group Analysis, Assoc. Member, Lincoln Institute for Psychotherapy

I write this commentary from my perspective as a group analyst and psychoanalytic psychotherapist with a past working experience of family therapy. I usually work with a co-therapist, which I prefer and which I think is preferable when working with couples. I see my theoretical perspective as based on theories of psychoanalytic couple therapy espoused by the Tavistock Institute of Marital Studies, the practice of group analysis of S.H. Foulkes and its development in work with families, couples and couples groups by A.C.R. Skinner. I am also influenced by family systems theory.

The Session

The session started with an interesting observation about the couple coming out of the lift, someone else in front of them: ‘This was extraordinarily perturbing’. It was not mentioned by the therapists again. Could it have been something to do with what was ultimately revealed to be Mrs Smith's concern, her husband's past suspected affair? My co-therapy partner's hypothesis was that it had to do with the couple's possible infertility; here was the unconceived baby in front of them at the lift.

One of my frustrations about the report was hearing nothing about the therapists' communications either during the session to each other, discussion after it or reported countertransference.

As you may have noted above co-therapy partners not only experience things differently but have different views, hear the material from varying perspectives according to their various qualities, experience, gender etc. In the case of this report a fruitful discussion ensued.

To my male partner the Smiths' keeping ‘at different ends of the house’, Mr Smith being ‘occupied’ (pre-occupied) ‘re-arranging the shelving’, ‘recharging himself’, his sensitive reactions to his wife over the phone: ‘what have I done?’ or ‘what have I not been able to do?’, all of this suggested the possibility that the couple were infertile, blaming each other and themselves. I had wondered about sexual difficulties underlying their conflict. Marrying these two points of view seemed fruitful. We were not necessarily dealing just with narcissistically vulnerable Mr Smith. We were seeing the impact of the interrelationship between inner worlds, the interpsychic system familiar to group analysts and couple therapists.

Psychic Security: Its Origins, Development and Disruption

Alfred Garwood

Alfred Garwood

Alfred Garwood  

The concept of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) has been belatedly recognized by its inclusion in DSM-III (APA 1980). It has spawned a substantial body of specialist literature in which, despite Freud having written ‘Psychoanalysis and War Neurosis’ in 1919, psychoanalytic theory is given scant attention. Freud suggested war neurosis was a form of traumatic neurosis characterized by ‘an alienation of the self, social withdrawal, irritability, recurrent dreams and flashbacks repeating the details of the experience, and severe anxiety’. Moore and Fine (1990) state that ‘efforts to relate the disorder to personality structure and function and to explain the symptomatology in terms of defences, gains and somatization have not been entirely satisfactory’. Traumatic neurosis is described as having two forms: the first being where trauma acts as the precipitating factor revealing a pre-existing neurotic structure, the second where the trauma is a decisive factor in the actual content of the symptoms i.e. ruminations over the traumatic events, recurring nightmares, and insomnia. The symptoms appear as a repeated attempt to bind and abreact the trauma; such fixation to the trauma are accompanied by a more or less general inhibition of the subject's activity. Psychoanalysts when speaking of traumatic neurosis are generally referring to the second form (Laplanche & Pontalis 1973).

A trauma implies an injury, but what has been injured? The clinical picture suggests this is psychic security. In this paper I wish to suggest this is a psychic entity, and to explore and describe the concept, its development, psychic elements, organization and disruption.

During my researches into Holocaust trauma it became clear that the central traumatizing experiences were 1. annihilation threat, 2. powerlessness and 3. object loss (Garwood 1996b). Pondering on why these were so powerfully traumatizing led me to focus on the earliest experiences of annihilation threat and powerlessness, the instinct for self-preservation and thus to the hypotheses that follow.

Susannah Izzard

Edgbaston, Birmingham B15 2TT. Email: s.a.izzard@bham.ac.uk

Susannah Izzard  

Although psychoanalysis has a new social consciousness regarding issues of homosexuality, the ramifications of new ways of thinking about these issues have yet to affect the theory of the Oedipus complex. To date there has been no review of the literature concerning the revision of developmental theory to reflect societal change and clinical insights into homosexuality. This article explores the options that are open to psychoanalytic thought in moving forward, by critically reviewing three different approaches to issues of development. Two main avenues seem open to the profession: to recapture the essence of Freud and retain an elaborated version of the Oedipus complex, or to argue that oedipal theory is so bound up with the socio-political culture of the day in t too, like the patriarchal context, must be abandoned.

Across the spectrum of diagnostic categories, patients allude in various ways to states of mind and emotion in which their autonomy is taken over to the detriment of their own goals and ambitions. These ‘take-overs’ happen within the therapeutic space or outside in the daily life of the patient, but a characteristic common to all is that they are experienced as outside the patient's control. A shortage in qualified psychotherapy supervisors in rural Norway motivated a study evaluating the quality of the supervision process when supervisors and trainees communicated by interactive audiovisual videoconferencing (VC). Six trainee and supervisor pairs participated in five alternating VC based and face-to-face sessions. The pairs had previously established a good face-to-face relationship. Self-report data of the quality of communication, the alliance and disturbing elements in the supervision sessions were collected from specially designed questionnaires completed after each session. Independent ratings of the videotaped sessions and qualitative interviews conducted at the end of the study were also conducted. The only significant difference between the two conditions was that trainees scored higher on disturbing factors under VC conditions. Recommendations for use of VC are provided in light of the findings. Key words: evaluation, psychotherapy supervision, quality, telepsychiatry.

Wilfred Bion's war service started when he signed on with the Inns of Court Officers Training Corps in January 1916 aged 18, shortly after leaving Bishops Stortford College. He was accepted by the gentlemanly Inns of Court through the influence of a friend of his father's. Shortly before this, he had presented himself on his own initiative, wearing his college cap. Among the parading recruits he was singled out by the sergeant:

‘You there - you with that college cap - 'op it.’

‘Can I go?’

‘Yus - that's wot I said - napoo - finished - rejected!’

(Bion 1982, p. 106)

By the end of 1916, there was official discouragement of under-age volunteers. After his father's intervention, he started training with the O.T.C. on Hampstead Heath, while living at home. His full-time service began with the Officer Training Unit, Bisley. After being commissioned he volunteered for the Machine Gun Corps (Heavy) - a euphemism for the still officially secret tank units of the British Army. His ultimate posting was to the 5th Battalion Tank Corps. At the Battle of Cambrai, he was awarded the D.S.O. and Legion of Honour. He had reached the rank of Captain by demobilization in 1919. He says that it was always assumed by himself and all concerned that he would be an officer. His writings in this volume are characteristically from this leadership perspective, which probably stayed with him throughout his life. In The Long Week-End he confessed to going into tanks attracted by ‘penetrating the secrecy of these newly-invented things’ (p. 115).

This book is quite a complex compilation, best understood with the aid of its editorial notes. It has been compiled and edited by Bion's widow, Francesca, to mark the centenary of his birth. It is in four main parts, drawn from Bion's own writings: Diary, France, 26 June 1917 to 10 January 1919; Commentary, 1972; Amiens, Prelude and Fugue (written 1958). In addition Aftermath, a brief review at the end, was written by Bion's daughter, Parthenope Bion Talamo, who was, as many will know, tragically killed in a road accident in 1998.

Editorial

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

No stronger impression arises from the resistances during the work of analysis than of there being a force which is defending itself by every possible means against recovery and which is absolutely resolved to hold onto illness and suffering… These phenomena are unmistakable impressions of the power in mental life which we call the instinct of aggression or of destruction according to its aims and which we trace back to the original death instinct of living matter… Only by the concurrent or mutually opposing action of the two primal instincts - Eros and death instinct - never by one or the other alone, can we explain the rich multiplicity of the phenomena of life. (Freud 1937, pp. 242-243)

How can we best explain ‘the rich multiplicity of the phenomena of life’ when there is so much ‘power in mental life’? How does the mind work? What model shall each of us find holds the best explanation? Whatever our views are about Freud, whether it makes sense to suggest that there is an ‘original death instinct of living matter’, or that we are caught between two opposing ‘primal instincts’, one thing that this issue testifies to is that the ‘power of mental life’ still confronts us anew each day as we work. We may argue for the exclusivity of our own theory under the belief that it alone seems to fit the phenomena better than another, but it is humbling to remember that when we write a paper we are struggling as best we can to ‘explain the rich multiplicity of the phenomena of life’.

First, Günter Seidler in ‘Destructive Narcissism and the Obliteration of Subject-Object Separation’ argues that we can explain destructive narcissism as the wish to obliterate all distinction between the subject and the object in order to return to a primordial place of peace. There is no need, in his theory, for destructive narcissism to be driven by a destructive instinct. Then Maggie Turp in ‘Encountering Self-Harm in Psychotherapy and Counselling Practice’ wants us to consider that ‘physical activity is not necessarily inimical to thoughtfulness’, as she seeks to understand why women harm themselves. She queries the accustomed psychoanalytic connection between thought and action, and concludes that ‘we might see self-harm as a kind of self-attention to the need for handling in order to stay alive’. Next, the way in which individuals can stay psychically alive under torture and oppression is the theme of Renos Papadopoulos's extended response, ‘Storied Community as Secure Base’ to Nancy Caro Hollander's paper ‘Exile: Paradoxes of Loss and Creativity’ that was published in BJP Vol. 15 No. 2. Hollander's paper was part of the Fifth Annual John Bowlby Memorial Lectures. I omitted to mention in my previous editorial that the John Bowlby Memorial Lectures are organized under the auspices of CAPP. Quite crucial to Papadopoulos's theory of survival is the concept of ‘shared narrative’. This concept carries the weight of several interlocking ideas, including attachment theory.

Gillian Hemmings

Gillian Hemmings

Gillian Hemmings  

Susan Kavaler-Adler, a psychoanalyst and founding director of the Object Relations Institute for Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis in New York, employs a rich and detailed theoretical and clinical knowledge of borderline phenomena in this, her second book on creativity. The major part is devoted to psycho-biographical speculations on female artists, followed by clinical illustrations.

She is particularly concerned with a pathological form of creativity which she calls ‘the Red Shoes frenzy’. Her concept grows from the 1948 film The Red Shoes (which is based on the Hans Christian Andersen tale), in which a young ballerina is enslaved by the power of her dance director (in the tale a shoemaker whose shoes she is literally unable to remove). In the film she is unable to give up the stardom offered by the director and thus unable to engage in and sustain a true and loving relationship in her interpersonal life. She is propelled to her death. This is the story of a woman who cannot experience her creativity as coming from within, but feels that it is dependent upon her external attachment to a god-muse. She is unable to separate from this fatherfigure and locate within herself her own split-off inner resources. She remains manically attached to him, impotent to assume a sense of agency, and lacks the sense of dwelling in herself that would enable her to maintain a good and loving relationship with an other (in the film, her husband). A dance to death seems inevitable.

The author sees ‘the Red Shoes frenzy’ as symbolizing a particular pathological constellation in which a part of the self becomes invested in a worship of one's own talents, rather than a participator in vibrant, sexually alive interpersonal relations.

[the] parents… [of] such [children] often have a basic narcissistic disregard for our primary emotional needs and disdain for human faults and vulnerabilities… For many artists… at least one primary parent served as a powerful mirror who reflected their talents, while disregarding the basic human needs for whole-object love. For such parents these needs threatened to interfere with the expression of the special talents of the child that mirrored the parents' narcissism providing an idealized glow that reflected back from the potential artist child towards the parent. (p. 55)

Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy12(3): 229-240, 1998

Bringing Deadness to Life: An Appreciation of Rosenfeld's Contribution to Thinking about Narcissism

Penelope Garvey

In this paper I have described some of Rosenfeld's ideas about narcissism, and in particular the distinction he makes between libidinal and destructive narcissism. Using a clinical example to illustrate the struggle between dependency and the power of excitement and destruction, I have attempted to show some narcissistic defences in action. I have argued that while Rosenfeld's differentiation may not hold, in that both constructive and destructive elements are always present, he has identified vividly important elements. The degree of the destructiveness, the extent to which it is split-off, hidden and unavailable, the extent to which it is maintained by excitement and eroticization, and the rigidity of the organization that has been set up (that is, whether or not much is allowed in from outside) are all crucial. What needs to be distinguished are states of mind, and which state of mind is in the ascendancy at any one time. I have reviewed briefly some of the theories advanced to explain why these defences come into existence, and I have mentioned some of the consequent implications for technique.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy12(3): 213-228, 1998

The Death Instinct: A Psychological Killer

Judith Felman

This paper considers the impact that a once-a-week therapy had on a patient with a borderline-narcissistic type of personality organization. The patient described, a 50-year-old woman, came to treatment following a depressive breakdown. The three-year period of psychotherapy seemed only to have made her de-compensate even further; her defensive organization continued to weaken. Yet, with the announcement of the end of treatment, a recovery started to occur. The theory of the life and death instincts, from its conceptualization and development by Freud, through its later evolution, is used as a conceptual framework to understand the powerful struggle within this individual between those forces pulling towards growth and development, and those pulling towards destructiveness and deterioration. The case is discussed not only with this theory in mind, but in the context of personality structure and of what happens when a patient's defensive organization is diminished through therapy. The ‘pros and cons’ of psychotherapy are considered, with special attention being paid to its implications for timelimited therapy within the NHS.
