Sigmund Freud's Programme for a Science of Consciousness

David Smith

David Smith

8 Brenchley Gardens, London, SE23 3QS. Email: 100131.575@compuserve.com

David Smith  

Sigmund Freud is best known as the creator of psychoanalysis. It is less widely appreciated that Freud's creation of psychoanalysis arose from his work in what is now called ‘cognitive science’ (Erdelyi 1985). Kitcher (1992) describes Freud as ‘the first’ interdisciplinary cognitive scientist (p. 5). Glymour (1991) states that ‘a big part of cognitive science is pretty much what you would expect to get if Sigmund Freud had had a computer’ (p. 44) and goes on to say that:

…Freud's writings contain a philosophy of mind, and indeed a philosophy of mind that addresses many of the issues about the mental that nowadays concern philosophers and ought to concern psychologists. Freud's thinking about the issues in the philosophy of mind is better than much of what goes on in contemporary philosophy, and it is sometimes as good as the best… Even when Freud had the wrong answer to a question, or refused to give an answer, he knew what the question was and what was at stake in it. And when he was deeply wrong it was often for reasons that still make parts of cognitive psychology wrong. (p. 46)

Freud is more widely regarded as a theorist of the unconscious than as a theorist of consciousness. In fact, Freud believed that any theory of unconscious mental states must address the problem of consciousness. Freud did just that, and his subtle and complex theorizing about consciousness is all too often neglected both inside and outside psychoanalysis. In particular, the new and rapidly growing academic discipline of ‘consciousness studies’ has neglected Freud's seminal contributions, many of which anticipate or even go beyond contemporary theorizing.1

In the present paper I will trace out some of the fundamental features of Freud's cognitive science of consciousness, with special emphasis on those aspects of it that dovetail with contemporary concerns in cognitive science, consciousness studies and the philosophy of mind. In order to do this I will contextualize Freud's theory of consciousness within the more general framework of the history of ideas and his overarching theory of the mental apparatus. 2 In the final part of the paper I will illustrate the continuing utility of Freud's approach by describing how it addresses an unresolved problem in consciousness studies: the widespread intuition that our inner lives conform precisely to folk psychological principles.

Cognitive-Analytic Therapy for Borderline Personality Disorder in the Context of a Community Mental Health Team: Individual and Organizational Psychodynamic Implications

Ian Kerr

Ian Kerr

Tooting, London SW17 7DJ

Ian Kerr  

Given that borderline personality disorder (BPD) is increasingly managed by community mental health teams (CMHTs), an exploration of the effectiveness of the cognitive-analytic model (Ryle 1997a) was undertaken in this context. A young man with a primary diagnosis of BPD was offered a course of cognitive-analytic therapy (CAT) by a member of the CMHT. Therapy was only partially successful, due apparently to the severity of the disorder but also, critically, to the absence of a shared understanding of the disorder by team members as well as other agencies involved. However, the CAT model, involving explicit reformulation, helped educate key members of the team about the disorder and the part they might play in it and to contain the splitting and anxiety provoked by such a patient. In addition, CAT created a reasonably robust therapeutic alliance, with more regular contact and no re-admission during the period of therapy. An extended ‘contextual’ reformulation can also offer a means of understanding the difficulties encountered in working with such patients, classically described by Main in ‘The ailment’ (1957), and provide the conceptual containment required to work with such ‘difficult’ patients.

Internal ‘Soul Murder’: An Impediment to Psychic Development

Julia Fabricius

Julia Fabricius

39 Willes Road, London, NW5 3D

Julia Fabricius  

The Oedipus complex remains central to human psychic development because the differences between the sexes and between the generations remain indisputable facts of life. Indisputable these facts may be, by the criteria of external, objective reality, but undeniable, by the criteria of human wishes, they are not, as any acquaintance with human kind, let alone any experience of patients in psychoanalysis, quickly and convincingly shows. It is the power of human denial, as well as its simultaneous ineffectiveness in reality, which gives analysis of the Oedipus complex the central place which it continues to hold in clinical practice.

In addition, failure to come to terms with these particular facts of life is a crucial matter for analysts because of the devastating effect this failure has on psychic development, in my view a life-long task and one which fundamentally involves separation-individuation (to use Mahler's term) from both external and internal objects. Failure of oedipal resolution is an intergenerational problem; it impedes both the development of the individual concerned, including in his analysis, and the development of his or her children. The manner of dealing with the Oedipus complex, by working through and mourning or by denial, is intimately associated with the manner of dealing with all the mourning involved in separation-individuation; ultimately, difficulty in achieving a degree of working through which is adequate for ongoing development always rests on a more general difficulty in acknowledging that an object is separate and independent from oneself (and therefore capable of having a relationship with a third object). This difficulty is the essence of a narcissistic mode of relating, one which seeks to prevent or deny autonomy.

In the patient I am going to present such difficulties could be seen clearly. Mr B appeared to have an internal model, which he did his utmost to preserve, of two objects, himself and another, existing inside one another. At the same time he strove to maintain a view of himself as without any attachment. I thought of the object with whom Mr B was thus entangled as broadly ‘maternal’ and saw his difficulty as being due to the lack of an internal father. The causes of his problem are not entirely clear but what is clear is the effect and the way the effect, in its turn, caused more of the same difficulty. His condition prevented him having what he needed, a third object to intervene with the inappropriately entangled pair. I shall try to show something of the circularity of the effects of his difficulty on his psychic development.

The encounters that are recorded in this book are the extended conversations that Anthony Molino had with each of five fellow analysts. In his Introduction he describes the aim of his book: ‘to provide, in a single collection, an overview of the lifework and thought of five of the most insightful and provocative thinkers in contemporary psychoanalysis’ (p. 2). They are all writers who have attracted Molino's interest and admiration and he sees them all as part of, or attracted to, the British Independent tradition, with Winnicott an important influence on them all. There are other links too: Phillips has edited Eigen, Bollas has promoted Coltart's writing in America. They all know and respect one another's work, Molino claims, and are thus genuinely ‘freely associated’.

Molino says that he was attempting an overview of the life and work of each of these writers. There are a number of books which review the work of a series of analytic writers and these are undoubtedly useful but can get very tedious, being endlessly descriptive. Molino's book would certainly fail if it was attempting to do overviews of that kind; what he does give us is far far better. Each conversation begins with Molino offering some thoughts he has had on the writer's recent work. The first few exchanges can be rather stilted and formal but, as both parties settle down, each conversation ranges off in different ways and in different directions. We all know that discourse between any two people is unique in its qualities and, although Molino provides ideas and topics, what we get from the subsequent self-expression of the subject is not an overview but rather a direct experience of what each writer is like, how they are and how they think, how truly individual each one is. This book is full of liveliness as each person, in his or her own unique way provides, as Molino says, ‘together with intellectual nourishment, inexhaustible sources of delight’ (p. 3). This sense of delight would be no less true of the conversation with Nina Coltart except that reading this now, after her death, is a more complicated experience, but I will return to this later.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

A question of perennial concern to philosophy is also one that has been an ongoing preoccupation of psychoanalysis and central to the therapies derived from it. This is the epistemological problem of how to emerge from the maze of the individual mind to engage with reality in such a way that new ideas are formed and learning takes place. Overcoming resistance to a new awareness of both internal and external reality is central to the therapeutic task, and is hindered by an incapacity to tolerate not knowing and by a rejection of otherness and difference. Further to the question and unique to the Freudian contribution to epistemology is the view that mental and emotional development requires that the individual be able to mourn and to truly give up what is irretrievably lost, unavailable or no longer of use, making space for the new.

Intimately connected with mourning is the establishment of a separate self in relation to separate others (or otherness), a necessary capacity in order to develop and to think. There are a multitude of ways to blur, deny or avoid separateness and loss, among them such phenomena as repeating past patterns and fixations in the transference, dependence on the therapist's authority, insisting that the world revolve around the self, or the various states of fusion or union with the other. Further psychoanalytic investigations into mental processes have found splitting and divisions within the self to be more common than Freud had thought. These splits are used to create defences against separateness by projection of parts of the self into others, attempts to control and possess the object through projective identification, or phantasies of living inside the object or the object living inside the self. The transference situation in psychotherapy is especially sensitive to revealing how the patient manoeuvres in order to deny separateness and otherness, and to avoid an encounter with a new unknown other.

When patients enter therapy they are often in the midst of traumatic or deeply unsatisfactory life situations. When the therapy situation enables them to recover and to initiate changes for the better, they often wish to leave before any fundamental internal change has taken place. Can they be shown possibilities for further development, of how the therapeutic relationship can help them to move towards true independence and creativity?

Synergy of Verbal and Non-Verbal Therapies in the Treatment of Mother-Infant Relationships

Helga Coulter and Elizabeth Loughlin

Elizabeth Loughlin

11 Oxford Street, South Yarra, Vic 3141, Australia

Elizabeth Loughlin  

The patient in the treatment of troubled mother-infant relationships is understood to be the lived relationship between mother and infant with the infant being an active participant in the relationship. As the infant is communicating in a non-verbal mode, a treatment medium is used that allows for both the active non-verbal contribution of the infant and the contribution of the mother, thus enabling both to work as their own therapists. Two different types of treatment modalities were combined: a psychoanalytically informed individual psychotherapy of mother and baby and a non-verbal approach of mother-infant dance therapy groups. An introductory overview of dance therapy specific to mother and infant is included as well as one case vignette and one case study. That it was the mother-infant dyad's physically meaningful experiences in the dance therapy group which acted as a catalyst for change became evident. The verbal treatment modality, on the other hand, was the essential understanding, metabolizing and containing space that sustained and consolidated these changes.

Even Paranoids Have Enemies: New Perspectives on Paranoia and Persecution edited by Joseph H. Berke, Stella Pierides, Andrea Sabbadini and Stanley Schneider. Published by Routledge, London, 1998; 233 pages; £15.99 paperback

John Clare

John Clare

John Clare  

‘Even paranoids have enemies’ is the reply Golda Meir is said to have made to Henry Kissinger during the Sinai talks when he accused her of being paranoid for hesitating to grant further concessions to the Arabs. This book, which came out of a conference to celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Arbours Association, looks at paranoia and persecution on many levels and aims to inform our thinking on the implications for social and ethical concerns and for clinical practice. The book is divided into three parts. Part I concentrates on the experience for the individual of external and internal persecution and on the therapeutic techniques needed to understand these complex issues. Part II examines paranoid processes in groups, institutions and bureaucracies. Part III looks at these themes in the cultural and political arena and considers moral panic and drugs legislation (Reefer Madness), the subjectivity of racism, machine phenomena in relationships, persecution in post-war Japan and a chapter on paranoia and the peace process. It is from the latter that the title of the book comes.

Throughout this eclectic and provoking set of essays we are moved to ruminate on the solutions to the Zeitgeist of persecution and suspicion at the end of the twentieth century. Salamon Resnik uses a meteorological model to define the atmosphere and tonality of the transference and shows how the emotionally cold climate of the paranoid psychotic renders those in his environment paralysed and frightened. Citing Freud's intuition with Frau P, he shows the importance of Verstehen (understanding rather than explanation) to map out the paranoid landscape. Thus he asks: when do the vision and climate of the world change from neurotic to psychotic? When does misunderstanding (based on otherness) turn into the unmistakable certainty of paranoia? While Bion believed that the weakness of the fact of transference is that it cannot be put into words, Resnik suggests that the climate of the analytic setting is a language in itself in which old patterns of family and culture are reproduced. In extending his hypothesis to the macro level of countries and culture, he considers the ‘basic personality’ of today. Whereas 50 years ago the ‘normal’ person of the Western world complied with the rules of existence in an obsessive manner, the ‘basic personality’ of recent years has become the paranoid one. This theme runs throughout the book, as it describes the dominance of paranoia as a social construction and its constellations as a mosaic of mind, individual and group.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Bion writes that the aims of psychoanalysis are to ‘introduce the patient to himself’ and, in time, to achieve ‘a sufficiently introjected capacity for learning from experience’. These are both simple and profound objectives, but is this science or is it art? Contributing to this eternal debate, Meg Harris Williams writes of the ideas of Bion and Meltzer that grasp the essential point that psychoanalysis is both an artistic and a descriptive-scientific endeavour: emotional truth is captured by artistic means while the truths gleaned will form a network of logical/scientific psychic fact. Thus, psychoanalytic method is an art form with the scientific aim of discovering personal truth and enduring truths about ourselves as human beings.

The main tools of our trade are words, and the meaning of words that refer to key concepts has been known to change over time. The terms we use to define mental phenomena gain (or lose) weight and depth as further observations are made and refinements of conceptualization take place. Thus, the term ‘projection’, which Freud used to refer to an important type of mental event, has developed since Freud to describe events of greater complexity, and now projective identification in turn has broadened in its meaning. It is presently thought to be an essential component of all communication. Carol Weaver in her article in this issue compares the concept of projective identification with that of intersubjectivity, demonstrating much similarity and overlap between the two.

Taking in the patient's projections for processing while, at the same time, juggling numerous other tasks in a limited space of time poses the challenge for the interviewer doing assessments for psychotherapy. Although some psychoanalysts do not believe in assessments, taking on allcomers, an assessment of suitability for treatment is a regular procedure for most psychotherapy services. This is in order to maximize the prospects for successful treatment in the face of limited availability, doing such things as matching up therapist and patient and preparing the patient for the work of therapy. Lorna Berger writes of how the countertransference of the assessor to the patient seeking therapy can importantly alter the dynamics of the interview, influencing both parties. Berger describes how the therapist's neurotic responses can be engaged to exert a constant pull on the assessor away from a position of a measured, objective judgement, inevitable yet requiring corrective vigilance on the part of the assessor.

An Examination of the Relationship between the Concepts of Projective Identification and Intersubjectivity

Carol Weaver MA

Carol Weaver

10 Fotheringhay, Peterborough PE8 5HZ. [email: CarolWeaver@compuserve.com]

Carol Weaver  

Projective identification has been described as ‘the most fruitful psychoanalytic concept since the discovery of the unconscious’ (Young 1994, p. 120). Many psychoanalysts, including Ogden, have also begun exploring the philosophical concept of intersubjectivity and how it may augment psychoanalytic understanding and practice. Existential psychotherapists include those who believe that intersubjectivity is the basic way in which humans relate. Diamond writes that ‘Without a notion of intersubjectivity, psychoanalysis is in difficulty, for it is impossible to envisage how feelings belonging to one individual pass into another’ (Diamond 1998, p. 202).

After exploring the concept of projective identification and the claims from various contemporary psychoanalysts that this mechanism is interpersonal rather than purely intrapsychic, the paper explores the philosophical concept of intersubjectivity. The communication of emotion and the implications for therapy are then discussed, before conclusions are drawn about the relationship between the two concepts under examination.

Profile of a Potential Abuser

Robin Balbernie

Robin Balbernie

Horton Road, Gloucester GL1 3PX

Robin Balbernie  

This is a study of a boy entering puberty who developed fantasies of sexually abusing younger children; it looks at a number of issues that lie behind such thoughts and the risk that they might be acted out. A child who has been the victim of inappropriate sexual advances from a parent may develop into an abuser themself later on in life, but this is not inevitable. Other risk factors have to be considered, and all taken in the context of the strong possibility that being exploited by a caregiver has left the child with neither a sense of trust nor an organized internal programme for creating fulfilling relationships (disorganized attachment) in the future. The six risk factors considered are: social isolation, unhelpful ego-defences, distorted identity, lack of empathy, a need to dominate, and precipitating oedipal fantasies into reality. Work with a boy in whom all six risk factors coalesced is described.

Introduction

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

We are used, in the UK, to thinking about the Holocaust in Europe, and the impact that it may have on survivors and members of the Second Generation who seek professional help. The paper which the Journal presents in the second part of our Australian section addresses an experience of the Holocaust at greater distance, both geographically and psychically.

The historian Esther Faye, in ‘“Enjoying” traumatically: the Holocaust as “the Second Generation”’ other', develops ideas initially presented at an international interdisciplinary conference in 1998 in Sydney (Faye 1998). ‘Trauma and Memory: Cross-Cultural Perspectives’, held under the auspices of the College of Fine Arts, University of New South Wales, and the Centre for Women's Studies, Australian National University, Canberra, aimed to explore the variety of languages - verbal, visual and performative -available for the articulation of traumatic memory. The context was the current exploration of the implications that traumatic events have for individual and collective memory, and the recognition of how much critical attention the experience of trauma has attracted in recent years, especially in regard to studies of the Holocaust and child sexual abuse. There were strands on post-Holocaust memory; cinematic responses to trauma, from Hiroshima to the gangsta rap film; the Stolen Generation in Australia; and bodily memory, the strand in which I was speaking.

A conference is an intense space, and it was brought home to me very vividly that an individual who is preoccupied with traumatic memory is part of a culture which is itself preoccupied with trauma and memory - be it in truth and reconciliation commissions, or Holocaust memorial, or contemporary film or art practice, or cultures of regret and apology. The conference brought these themes together; inevitably it staged an encounter between them. It illustrated the intensification of narrative possibilities in cultures that increasingly validate a language of trauma.

‘Enjoying’ Traumatically: The Holocaust as ‘The Second Generation's’ Other

Esther Faye

Esther Faye

Clayton, Melbourne, Victoria 3168, Australia. [email: esther.faye@arts.monash.edu.au]

Esther Faye  

This paper sets out to explore a question opened up by the growing number of life-writings and oral testimony currently being produced by members of ‘the second generation’. That is, how can the descendants of Jewish Holocaust survivors free themselves from ‘the repetition of suffering’, which, in the language of Lacanian psychoanalysis, could be described as the attachment to an unbearable form of enjoyment (jouissance) of the Shoah? The paper pursues a Lacanian reading of the writing of one such descendant, the expatriate Australian writer, Lily Brett. It considers whether the themes of anxiety, death, eating, bodies and the fantasy of love between mothers and daughters that structure her stories constitute a form of testimony with, as the Lacanian Israeli psychoanalyst Rivka Warshawsky puts it, ‘the power of resolving the repetition compulsion’.

Sasha Brookes  

This article offers a psychoanalytic reading of Henry James's well-known ghost story, The Turn of the Screw, an ambiguous and fascinating tale narrated by a young governess put in sole charge of two orphan children. Henry James was an early modernist in the sense that he required his readers to think about his text and interpret it for themselves. In this tale he engages the reader's interest in haunting in the story and in general, and raises the question of where ghosts are to be found: in inner or in outer reality? The ghosts of the tale have intense relationships and interchanges with some of the living characters, and the article suggests that the ‘ghosts’ may be understood as the characters' split-off and projected experiences of loss. These return to haunt them, in spite of their strenuous efforts to defend themselves against the pain of bereavement and loss of omnipotence. As James says, the presence of the children in the story makes more poignant the return of the uncontained projections in the form of nameless dread.

This is an eminently sensible book. It is a measure of the maelstrom surrounding the issue of recovered memories and their validity that to invoke commonsense as the consummate criterion by which to judge this book is intended as the highest praise, not as a faint commendation elliptically implying want of imagination, passion or empathy. On the contrary, each of the 16 contributions movingly exhibits these qualities, but leaves the reader with a sense of balanced containment. In his careful foreword where he talks of ‘something akin to a religious war raging between those who wish to protect the victims of childhood abuse and those whose declared allegiance is to individuals claiming to be falsely accused’ (p. xiv), Peter Fonagy sets the tone:

It is a challenge to all of us to preserve precious doubt in a situation where we are under pressure from our clients, from their relatives and from the general public to adopt a clear position; however, when clarity can only be achieved through extremism, the price is too high - the sacrifice of individual lives is intolerable. (p. xv)

Valerie Sinason's introduction picks up this refrain about the need to combine intellectual doubt with empathic response, while giving important information on what might be called the politics of the dispute about memories. She describes how parents, smarting from the feeling of being wrongly accused, developed the False Memory Syndrome Foundation in the USA and the British False Memory Society (BFMS) in the UK.

Patterns of missed appointments and fee payments for six female clients who were in therapy for one year or more prior to the therapist's pregnancy were studied. The study revealed that there were significant differences in appointments missed and no significant differences in fee-paying patterns during and following the pregnancy when compared to patterns prior to the pregnancy. The changes in appointment patterns can affect the therapist's attitude toward clients and intensify a sense of instability. Anticipation of such changes can prevent unnecessary stress for both the client and therapist.

Joseph Sandler

Rosine Perelberg

Rosine Perelberg

Rosine Perelberg  

This is an extremely sad occasion for me. It is also an honour to be asked to say a few words about Joe, as I feel that so many of you here today would have so much to say about the ways in which he has had an impact on you and your thinking. Anne-Marie, the family, and the British Society itself have received hundreds of letters expressing feelings of great loss.

Joe Sandler was one of the most outstanding contemporary thinkers in psycho-analysis. Colleagues and friends from around the world have been in a state of shock, since they received the news of his terminal illness just a few weeks ago. As you know, just 15 days earlier Joe Sandler had delivered a paper at a conference at the British Psycho-Analytical Society in honour of Hanna Segal, an esteemed colleague and friend. This was an expression of his generosity to his friends, but also a testimony that he was thinking and working until the very end. He received so many prizes and honorary doctorates, an international recognition that went back to the early years when he was awarded the prestigious Union of South Africa Scholarship, which allowed him to come to England.

Joseph Sandler made fundamental contributions to both the theory and practice of psychoanalysis with his wisdom and incomparable understanding of psychoanalytic ideas and concepts, which he helped to elaborate. He had a profound understanding that symptoms were expressions of and solutions for conflicts, and insisted that his students fully understood that. This deep understanding of human nature and respect for his patients was expressed in his practice of psychoanalysis: he stressed the part played by feelings of well-being in the regulation of mental functioning. Each individual develops coping mechanisms in the face of helplessness in order to feel safe. Symptoms may be understood as the individual's attempt to provide a protective shield in order to maintain an experience of psychic equilibrium. This obviously does not always work, a fact which is what brings the patients to treatment. In his book What Do Psychoanalysts Want? Joe Sandler argued that the aim of psycho-analysis is to help patients accept unacceptable, infantile parts of themselves which have aroused painful conflicts. This idea was central to his supervision and teaching.

On Hallucination, Intuition, and the Becoming of ‘O’ by Eric Rhode. Published by ESF Publishers, Binghamton, New York, 1998; 230 pages; paperback

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

Meg Williams  

One of Bion's well-known jokes was that he suspected he would be among those who are ‘loaded with honours and sunk without trace’. And probably he would have been, had not Donald Meltzer led the way in persistent deep-sea diving of his works. Now, despite the weight of establishment honours (which usually take the form of explaining how Bion's ideas are really just badly expressed commonsense), the body refuses to go down. And certainly Eric Rhode must be reckoned among the idiosyncratic deep-sea divers who have bravely entangled themselves in Bion's mesh. Or - to use another of Bion's metaphors - he is one of those tomb-robbers who broke through the magical prohibitions at Ur. ‘Don't go down the unconscious, Daddy!’ spoke his warning voice (Bion 1982, p. 143).

Any interpretation of Bion which is not establishment is idiosyncratic. Bion has ensured that he cannot be read in any other way. The tomb-robbing analogy is as good an entry as any to the fascinating content of Rhode's book. For much of the material which Rhode explores here is anthropological in nature, the result of his study of primitive ancient Egyptian and African cultures, in search of a long-buried ‘religious’ vertex which in Bion's view has been much neglected ever since psychoanalysis replaced religious problems by sexual ones. The religious vertex makes ‘holes’ in what appears to be a smooth continuum of ‘scientific’ knowledge, and to research it Rhode makes use of a mixture of personal ‘reverie’ and anthropological interpretation. We remember Bion's view that thinking begins at a point where psyche and soma start to differentiate. Somewhat analogously, Rhode's approach is to tap the primitive realms where psychotic and nonpsychotic are not much differentiated. He investigates the roots of religion and the struggles of primitive peoples and ancient civilizations to create symbols rather than fetishes - one might say to use imagination rather than hallucination.

When a symbol is created, it reverberates both backwards and forwards in time. Rhode cites a Benin musician whose visit to the Paris opera put him ‘bang in the middle of a possession ceremony’ (p. 196).

This essay considers Bion's and Meltzer's enumeration of both artistic and scientific qualities inherent in psychoanalytic practice in relation to the problem of learning from experience. Their work encourages practitioners to value the liberating potential of psychoanalysis as an art form. This is emphasized through the complex cognitive implications of Bion's ‘reverie’ and Meltzer's ‘aesthetic conflict’, suggesting that psychoanalytic advance will consist in the marriage of artistic modes of cognition with a scientific body of knowledge.

Getting Rid of Oedipus: The Impossible Solution

Gigliola Spoto

Gigliola Spoto

101 Camberwell Grove, London SE5 8JH

Gigliola Spoto  

Introduction

Psychoanalysts believe that the negotiation of the Oedipus complex is an essential developmental task which shapes and structures psychic reality, and which promotes growth and maturation. The Oedipus complex is at its heart a struggle between love and hate, which every human being has to engage in, when the narcissistic illusion of exclusive access to and possession of the primary object has to be relinquished.

A successful outcome of this struggle defines the psychic structure of the individual, establishes the difference between the sexes and the generations, promotes a move towards psychic separateness out of the mother/infant dyad and contributes to the establishment of symbolic capacities.

The move from illusion to reality is not a painless or a straightforward one. Melanie Klein (1928), who connects the Oedipus complex with the epistemophilic instinct (in particular curiosity for the mother's body and its contents, which include babies and the father's penis), emphasizes how the ‘…ego is still so little developed when it is assailed by the onset of the Oedipus tendencies and the incipient sexual curiosity associated with them’. The infant, like Oedipus trying to find out about his origins, is exposed to an ‘onrush of problems and questions’, but also confronted with his impossibility to know, because of his intrinsic position of smallness and helplessness.

The story of Oedipus is poised between the impossibility to know and the necessity to know. Money-Kyrle (1964) says that: ‘Oedipus epitomizes man at a critical stage of his development, when he is faced by a choice, that between self-knowledge and self-deception.’ Seen like this, the oedipal story can be thought of paradigmatic of the task that every analysand undertakes when he or she embarks on an analytical journey, and some of its centrality in analytical thinking derives from the fact that it symbolizes the complex endeavour to reach emotional truth about oneself and one's objects.

The need to know and the opposite need not to know runs powerfully through the oedipal story, as does the final ‘unavoidability’ of the truth. Laius's efforts to get rid of Oedipus lead to his own tragic demise in their fated encounter, equally Oedipus will be forced to accept the true story about himself. Steiner (1993) (using the Oedipus of the Sophoclean tragedies) has spoken of Oedipus's tendency to self-deception, and described it as a ‘turning a blind eye’. Fainberg (1993, using Robert Graves's 1955 version of the Oedipus myth) focuses on the other characters of this evocative story, mainly Laius and Jocasta, and comments that deceit and lies and refusal of the truth are paramount in the whole story: Oedipus has deceitful parents as his ‘oedipal objects’.

Storied Community as Secure Base: Response to the Paper by Nancy Caro Hollander ‘Exile: Paradoxes of Loss and Creativity’

Renos Papadopoulos

Renos Papadopoulos

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Renos Papadopoulos  

Nancy Hollander's (1998) paper is both important and topical despite the fact that it refers to historical events which are not very recent. Its importance lies in the fact that it addresses the crucial facet of analytical theory and practice which relates to wider societal dimensions as well as to social action. This is a thorny facet which never loses its topicality because, as analysts, we constantly face the challenge as to how to reconcile our position in response to violations of freedom, human dignity and justice in socio-political contexts, outside our consulting rooms. Although her paper refers to the political turmoil and oppression in one specific region, that of Central and South America, the same challenge is posed wherever there are violations of human rights. Moreover, similar concerns exist in all societies at all times, in connection with relatively minor incidents and circumstances where, nevertheless, ethical and moral issues are at stake. In these situations, the principles remain the same, regardless of the scale and specificity of the occasion.

The dilemma we face in relation to this kind of challenge questions some fundamental assumptions about the nature of the analytical enterprise. Psychodynamic theories, as they are applied to traditional analytical settings, tend to be based on a paradigm which is predominantly formulated within a pathology/deficit model, and which emphasizes the intrapsychic dimension at the expense of the social realities. How, then, can theories and practices which emanate from such a paradigm be in a position to offer us anything of relevance in turbulent socio-political contexts?

In response to this challenge, Hollander turns to attachment theory with her own selective emphasis and modifications, which she presents in a personal, moving and poetic style. Her choice of attachment theory fits well with the material she discusses, and her selection of personal narratives of survivors and victims of oppression to illustrate her position is equally appropriate and successful. My own response to her paper is in line, by and large, with her overall approach and is intended to explore certain implications of her stance. More specifically, I shall develop some ideas about the meaning of shared narratives and how these can extend our understanding of Bowlby's theories about the secure base.

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini  

Mary - a schizoid artist for whom therapy functioned as a bridge between a rich inner world ‘blessed, or cursed, with a surcharge of runaway creative energy’ (p. 139), and a depressingly dull external life.

Dan - a would-be rock star who believed he was being tape-recorded by his therapist and whose psychotic pathology deteriorated into fully-fledged paranoid episodes. His analyst joined him as a companion into his delusional system, in an attempt to help him become more empathic to his own intrapsychic and interpersonal persecutory objects.

Katherine - an ‘emotionally volatile, manic actress who acted out her rage at having to be a waitress by pouring coffee on a customer's coat’ (p. 31). Her therapist was amazed by the remarkably few credits she could show after 12 years' labour Off-Off Broadway, in spite of her obvious talents, and ‘the low priority she put on relationships that lay outside the sphere of her art’ (p. 39).

Steve - a musician who invited his analyst to his debut concert as a solo pianist. ‘He walked sheepishly across the bare stage,’ his therapist vividly recounts. ‘Seating himself at the piano, Steve suddenly - with his familiar self-torturing indecisiveness - began to wonder if the height of his stool was correct. For about two minutes, as the audience waited, Steve repeatedly raised the stool, then lowered it…’ (p. 5). As soon as he started playing, he was transformed into a self-confident, competent professional delivering ‘a dazzling exhibition of performing virtuosity’ (p. 5).

Harry - a playwright dying of brain cancer who, using denial as his main defence, impressed and moved his therapist with the ‘unwavering single-mindedness with which [he] seemed to be carrying out his soldierly resolve to live his life as independently as he could right up until the end’ (p. 118).

Gerald Alper - a psychotherapist who practised at the New York City Community Guidance Service where he acquired the unique clinical experience of analysing young, talented, aspiring and often poor artists, such as musicians, writers, actors and painters, mostly presenting symptoms of work inhibition, narcissistic depression, creative blocks and paralysing feelings of inner deadness. The case histories that constitute the bulk of the book - Mary, Dan, Katherine, Steve, Harry - are powerfully written in a literary style comparable to Robert Lindner's popular The Fifty-Minute Hour (1954) and reflecting Alper's own experience as an author of fiction.

Patricia Marsden and J. Lacey MD M Phil. FRCPsych

J. Lacey

Cranmer Terrace, London SW17 ORE. [email: pmarsden@sghms.ac.uk]

J. Lacey  

The cases of two pairs of female monozygotic twins concordant for anorexia nervosa are considered in order to explore the interrelationship between the psychodynamics of the twin relationship and the psychopathology of anorexia. It is suggested that twins face a dual task of separation-individuation - from mother and from the other twin - and that separation-individuation between monozygotic twins presents particular difficulties. Anorexia nervosa may represent an attempt to avoid separation by means of a retreat to a pre-adolescent state in which differences, envy and rivalry can be denied.

Commentary by a Psychoanalytic Individual and Marital Psychotherapist

Monica Lanman

Monica Lanman

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3

Monica Lanman   Member of the British Association of Psychotherapists, Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists, Society of Psychoanalytic Marital Psychotherapists

It is an interesting challenge to be invited to comment on material from a session without any background introduction to the case. But in terms of this session I think this is a patient couple who are helpfully persistent in describing their difficulties

87

despite their being different to an important degree from those which the therapists interpret. On the other hand the therapists seem to me to be persistently missing opportunities to grasp the key to this session as it appears both indirectly in the material and directly in the here and now of the transference relationship.

In the first paragraph one phrase leaps off the page, ‘extraordinarily perturbing’. It is not elaborated, but I take it that the therapists felt perturbed by the lift event, since there is no material about the patients' reaction to it. The therapists apparently didn't think about this feeling and try to use it in the session. I would see it as countertransference, possibly reflecting a relationship both between the couple and between the patient couple and the therapist couple, which is experienced as fused, in which an obstacle to instant connection between therapists and patients is felt to be extraordinarily disturbing. Next, and connecting with this thought, I wonder why the patients shake hands with the therapists at the start of every session (this is clearly not the first). And why they still have to be met at the lift. Is there an enactment of something infantile here, and anxiety about not being able to trust a different kind of emotional contact if immediacy and touch are not maintained? I think the later material about the couple having to phone each other constantly resonates with this.

Mr and Mrs S say there are no traumas to report, and I wonder if this means they have been ‘playing safe’ and avoiding conflict for some reason. The word ‘trauma’ itself suggests an awareness of trauma even as it is being denied. The therapist goes straight into offering an interpretation, apparently without any invitation to Mr S to elaborate. Is there an anxiety here which the therapists get caught up in, that opening things up would be threatening?

Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel  

Rather than take up the habitual objections to Kleinian and object relations theorists' conceptions of the Oedipus complex, a discussion is presented of two current ‘models’: the Anti-Oedipus and the American relational perspective. Considered as utopias (the utopia of limitless, unconstrained pleasure and the egalitarian utopia), these ‘models’, which apparently stand opposed, are shown to be sustained by a common underlying fantasy, that of a psyche without structure or organization. A relationship is established between the birth of the psychic apparatus and the oedipal configuration which can also be found in the classical analytic situation as well as in the biblical myth of Genesis.

Assessment - What for? Who for?

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

58 Roupell Street, London SE1 8TB

Josephine Klein  

It is customary for psychotherapists to write diagnostic assessments on prospective patients, either for their own use or for the use of those to whom the patient is referred for treatment. But our theories are not sufficiently advanced for such assessments to be very useful in indicating suitable treatment accurately. Indeed, on the whole, assessors refer patients to colleagues trained as they were trained, Freudians to Freudians, Kleinians to Kleinians, Gestalt to Gestalt, cognitive to cognitive, or else they refer according to the requirements of the institution they work in. Diagnosis does not indicate treatment in any generally agreed way.

Two attempts at a more systematic approach are sketched but, while we are waiting for diagnostic theory to catch up to the point where we can use it for therapy, some interim measures are suggested which would do more justice than is now done, both to the variety of human distress and the variety of therapeutic procedures currently available.

The Absent Father and His Return: Echoes of War

Gertrud Mander Dr phil

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NWI 8YD

Gertrud Mander  

The trauma of the past, the echoes of war - how do we become aware of these in our work with individuals who as children suffered the consequences of their parents' war experiences, and how do we conceptualize the damaging effects of the parents' emotional wounds inflicted on the second or third generation? Much work has been done with Holocaust victims and the second generation and there are revealing American studies of Vietnam War veterans. But it took 70 years and a work of fiction to remind us of the beginnings of therapeutic treatment for shell shock in World War I. On the basis of extensive clinical material this paper attempts to describe some pathogenic effects exerted by the transmission of war trauma from fathers to children, speculates about the legacy of this century's terrible war and wonders how we are dealing with this in our therapeutic work.

[[RunningHead]]

A Memoir of My Psychoanalysis with Dr Clara Geroe

Deirdre Moore

Deirdre Moore

1/530 Tooronga Road, East Hawthorn, Vic. 3123, Australia

Deirdre Moore  

We're grouped around the table, hunched and intense. We are a Study Circle, the Melbourne Psychoanalytic Study Circle of 1949. The postal address which used to be 111 Collins Street is now swallowed up in the multi-storey skyscraper of the Grand Hyatt Hotel, Melbourne.

It is a small room, and seems smaller, crowded with eight or ten people. The ambience is post-Hapsburg central European: our teacher and spiritual guru, Dr Clara Lazar-Geroe, comes straight out of the late Austro-Hungarian Kultur. Her brightly coloured, heavily embossed embroideries cover the cushions and side-tables, and there is a Persian carpet. She speaks English with a heavy Hungarian accent.

We're all dedicated. The three psychiatrists present include one who practises at Pentridge prison, the main prison for serious offenders, in the north-west area of Melbourne. The women include a teacher who runs a progressive school in the country who, in her haste, has not had time to wash her mud-spattered ankles, and the heavily pregnant psychologist whose toddler is with the babysitter. We have completed or are completing our training analyses. Most of us know only too well the brown leather closely buttoned couch in the next room, and the 50-minute hour.

Like all fundamentalists, we use symbolic language and the words of the Master: our text book The Collected Papers of Sigmund Freud (then in four volumes). For these erudite and expensive texts we are saving up. We grapple with the Master's Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex (1938), and, specifically, with contribution two: Infantile Sexuality, proposed in 1905.

‘Cruelty appears in the child before pity,’ says Dr Clara Geroe in her soft-spoken, ever-patient way. ‘A child cannot pity something unless he has been cruel to it first.’ The socialists among us are horrified. ‘Pity is, in the first place, a reaction formation against the parents’ disapproval of the baby's cruel and aggressive behaviour towards something, ‘she continues’.

The teacher soaks it up. At her boarding-school, run on Freudian principles of the Thirties as embodied in the New Education Fellowship (Susan Isaacs, Melanie Klein), some of her pupils are problem children culled from mainstream schools, some are not. She asks questions about them in discussion. She is training to become a lay child analyst.

Clinical Material: Mr and Mrs Smith

Mr and Mrs Smith arrived on time. Someone else came out of the lift in front of them. This was extraordinarily perturbing. Mr and Mrs Smith shook hands with each of us as usual.

In the room, both looked fairly relaxed. Mr Smith began. There were no traumas to report. Mrs Smith agreed. Mr Smith said awkwardly that, of course, this should be the case. There did not have to be a crisis or dramatic event. But he worried about our time when there was not much to say. Therapist A said that, if there was not a trauma or a crisis, was it worth coming? Would it justify our time if there was nothing dramatic to report? Mr Smith said that it was something like that. Mrs Smith looked relaxed and nodded in agreement. Mr Smith said that he had noticed on the way here that there was not much that he wanted to say; there had not been any major arguments.

Mrs Smith then said, affably, but in a way that made Mr Smith wince, that they had not of course seen much of one another to argue. They had both spent lots of time in the house but at different ends. He had been occupied in his workroom rearranging the shelving. Mrs Smith laughed. Mr Smith explained that he had been at home for a few days holiday. He admitted that he was in the workroom a lot of the time. Sometimes he needed space and this was his way of recharging himself. Mrs Smith accepted that he needed a complete break but there were all sorts of jobs that she needed doing, things to be sorted out in the kitchen. She accepted that Mr Smith needed his rest, saying that these jobs could wait.

The Memory Bird: Survivors of Sexual Abuse edited by C. Malone, L. Farthing and L. Marce. Published by Virago, London, 1997; 336 pages; £8.95

Valerie Sinason

Valerie Sinason

London

Valerie Sinason  

This anthology has been written cooperatively by abuse survivors - men and women, able-bodied and physically disabled, of different religious, racial and social class backgrounds. It is written in prose, free verse, rhyming verse, poetry, diary, art and words. It tells of abuse from within the family (siblings, parents and grandparents) and from trusted authority figures (teachers, scoutmasters.) It tells of abuse in private in the home, of group abuse, of satanic abuse. It recounts narratives of pain that left the writers suicidal, stupefied, depressed, self-injuring, at the mercy of substance abuse or abusive relationships. It left some to the mercy of poor health service treatment, whether inpatient psychiatry or therapy, whilst others thankfully received life-saving treatment (Childline, individual or group therapy, counselling). It is a searing and powerful testimony of loss, hurt, betrayal and resilience.

The sections into which the book is divided provide a guide to the main themes: The Blades of My Life (living with pain), The Survivor's Song (belonging and relationships), Claiming the Right to Feel Pain, Pulling Things from a Dark Cupboard (remembering), Can You Hear Me? (silences), Turned on a Tide (transition), Learning to Dance (beginning to feel), Eating the Coal (oppressions), You Want a Witness? (the role society and institutions play) and, finally, Us (personal statements).

One contributor, Gill de la Cour, a professional counsellor working with clients who have experienced abuse and also a survivor, lucidly points to the fake splits between ‘experts’ and ‘survivors’, the prejudiced implication being that experts are not survivors. Splitting is an inevitable consequence of abuse for the child, the adult, the wider society and also perhaps the readers of this book. I initially began to read this book split between myself as a poet, a poetry teacher for those who use writing as healing, for those who aim to be professional poets (Art) and as a therapist working with victims and survivors - to name but a few.

Freud, Jung, Klein: The Fenceless Field by Michael Fordham, edited by Roger Hobdell. Published by Routledge, London, 1998; viii and 284 pages; £15.99 paperback

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers  

Michael Fordham was a father to analytical psychology in the United Kingdom: like most fathers, he was good and bad, deeply loved and deeply hated. There is no doubt that this son of landed gentry, who lost his own mother at the age of 15 and never got over it, did pioneer a particular version of child analysis. He founded the Society of Analytical Psychology, started its Journal and, with Gerhard Adler and Herbert Read, edited the English translations of Jung's Collected Works. He was a remarkable pioneer. Like most frontiersmen he could be ornery, awkward and just plain cussed when he put his mind to it. This is cheerfully reflected in the idiosyncratic reviews and letters which form the third section of the book.

This, his last work, collects essays and teachings from a long and distinguished career. It contains an invaluable bibliography and is well indexed. There is a special hubris in the title. The not-so-hidden message is ‘Klein is to Freud as Fordham is to Jung’. Both claimed fame through work with children; both made brilliant theoretical leaps on the basis of deep intuitions; both produced ideas which recent advances in developmental and experimental psychology have not entirely substantiated (though it is unlikely that that discipline would be where it is now without these two to quarrel with). Sadly, both also succeeded in splitting their analytic societies into still-feuding bits due to their abrasive personalities and haughty preference for ‘being right’ instead of ‘being reasonable’. It isn't possible to be a Jungian in London without meeting ‘Fordham's analytic family’. Roger Hobdell, a loyal son, has done an excellent job of collating and arranging to guide us into and through Fordham's thinking.

The first section gives an historical background. The essay ‘Freud, Jung and Klein’ is a five star piece; a clear exposition of the similarities and differences between two traditions in depth psychology, with a masterly, readable comparison of Jung's and Klein's basic concepts. It's hard to fault, and deserves a place on the reading lists of every student of psychotherapy, whether humanistic or ‘trad’. In the second chapter, ‘Identification’, he suggests Freud the neurologist favoured a tabula rasa picture of the psyche. Jung, a practising psychiatrist and famous experimental psychologist, was appropriated by Freud (Taylor 1996). As a biological scientist, Jung naturally inclined towards strongly developmental, phylogenetic models of mind - the whole potential of each human is present at birth as genetic information which ‘unpacks’ during development.

Encountering Self-Harm in Psychotherapy and Counselling Practice

Maggie Turp

Maggie Turp

73 Torbay Road, London NW6 7DU. email: MaggieTurp@aol.com

Maggie Turp  

This paper offers a perspective on self-harm as encountered by psychotherapists and counsellors practising in non-institutional settings. The author notes that the background of epidemiological information, which might inform clinical practice with these clients, is far from satisfactory. Difficulties in establishing an accurate epidemiology of self-harm are considered. Some common responses to incidents of selfharm are then explored, with particular reference to countertransference issues and the lack of containment (Bion 1962) available to practitioners in some professions.

A brief overview of theoretical perspectives on self-harm is followed by a more detailed account of the contributions of Welldon (1988), Bion (1962, 1967) and Winnicott (1949, 1962, 1967). The author describes and discusses her work with clients who harm themselves, drawing primarily upon the concepts of ‘projective identification’ (Klein 1946), ‘containment’ (Bion 1962) and ‘psychosomatic indwelling’ (Winnicott 1967).

Assessment: The Struggle towards Objectivity

Lorna Berger

Lorna Berger

122 St Albans Avenue, Chiswick, London W4 5JR

Lorna Berger  

In this paper I aim to explore the dynamics inherent in the assessment process, with particular reference to the therapist's overall emotional response. This response is composed of the therapist's more personal, subjective feelings, as well as their countertransference. Under the pressure exerted by a limited time frame (one interview) and the magnitude of the task, the therapist's contribution to the dynamics will be significant and, I will argue, mutative, affecting the patient's behaviour and thus the direction of the interview. This will have an effect on the assessor's conclusions and recommendation.

The paper describes the therapist's struggle to maintain an observing stance, and to think psychodynamically and diagnostically, when meeting with a stranger at assessment.

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

56 Osbaldeston Road, London N16 7DR

Marguerite Valentine  

Money is significant in many relationships, including that of psychotherapy. Yet within analytic writing it is often neglected. The early writings of Freud and Ferenczi are somewhat limited in identifying its potential importance, compared perhaps with Winnicott's exploration of its transactional significance within an object relations framework. Perhaps surprisingly, the early philosophical writings of Karl Marx, as he struggled to understand the symbolic importance of money in terms of its power to represent alienation and objectification, indicate a possible way of developing further understanding. The paper illustrates some of these points with two clinical case discussions.

Günter Seidler  

The article describes the specific psychodynamics of ‘destructive narcissism’, a configuration which in its effects, if not in its intentions, can truly be said to be ‘destructive’. The two most widely used diagnostic manuals (ICD-10 and DSM-IV) correctly deny it the status of an illness or personality disorder in its own right, as it is more appropriately described as a fundamental anthropological dimension. As such it is similar in status to consciousness, bipersonal reciprocity or self-referentiality. Its aim is the obliteration of the subject-object relation. Destructive narcissism finds expression in a variety of manifestations differing according to context. They include some psychic symptoms and disorders. The article is also a plea for the application of psychoanalysis (enriched by a phenomenological perspective) to the discussion of anthropological issues.

Betty Joseph

Betty Joseph

Betty Joseph  

Parthenope Bion Talamo died tragically in a car accident in July 1998, along with her younger daughter Patrizia aged 18, Parthenope herself being 53. I had known her since she was about 3 and although at times we might not meet for long periods we somehow always remained in contact. In her early years she and her father lived in Iver, Buckinghamshire; I got to know her as her father and I were students together at the Institute of Psycho-Analysis. Parthenope was a striking and determined little girl even then and managed to start school on her own initiative as the school was next door to their home and she climbed through a hole in the intervening hedge.

Parthenope is probably best known in England for her writing and lecturing about her father and his work but she was also, I believe, a gifted and concerned clinician. Although many people may have heard her speak on various occasions she was probably not well known personally here as she had lived for many years in Italy, in Turin, and was a member of the Italian Society.

She had a very sad beginning: her mother died a few days after her birth, and for her early years she was looked after by a simple but very devoted housekeeper. When she was 6 her father remarried and the family moved to Croydon. Here her brother Julian - now a consultant anaesthetist - and sister Nicola were born. Understandably she did not find life easy and as a child went into analysis with Lois Munro - an analysis about which she always spoke most warmly as an adult.

As she grew up it was clear she was the kind of person who would find her own way in life, and she loved travelling, sometimes alone as she did one year in Turkey, to her family's considerable consternation. But she always kept in close contact with the family, especially I think with her father. She went for a short period to Italy to improve her Italian and study art history and then decided to go to university in Florence, where she read philosophy and psychology. Here she met her future husband, Luigi, a most talented musician, and they set up home in Rome. She followed her interest in psychology, went into analysis with Adda Corti and then, when her husband was appointed to the position of first viola in the RAI orchestra in Turin, they moved to Turin, to her great pleasure. From here, despite the considerable travelling difficulties, she took the analytical training in Milan.

Jonathan Sklar

Jonathan Sklar

London

Jonathan Sklar  

This is a small and yet very impressive book. Ending analysis is an extremely important area of work. Its very nature means that knowledge in this area is not available to the student during psychodynamic training. Of course, theory can be read but to experientially and affectively feel the subject when one is in the middle of one's own analysis and the work of one's training patients is probably nearly impossible. This, then, is essential work in training that can really only be left beyond the end of training and to be perceived in the very ending of one's own analysis. This is a problem that Gilda de Simone uncovers in swift decisive chapters, which do not give space for any ‘rules of ending’. Instead thinking is opened up to examine many essential analytic conundrums, all of which suffuse the final movement of the work with the patient.

Ending analysis is examined around the central paper of ‘Psychoanalysis Terminable and Interminable’ (Freud 1937). Early in the book Freud's pessimism is contrasted with Ferenczi's optimism (Ferenczi 1927). Various theories are spun for the reader, with ideas moving from early analytic theory as solution to conflict, to the complexities of the patient-analyst dyad, transference and countertransference. All the while ‘Nachtraglichkeit’, the reworking of every psychic experience in the light of new experiences and access to further development, is a core argument in relation to thinking about the ending.

In the book, technique is considered in relation to theories. Who decides the ending? Freud famously terminated the Wolfman's treatment and this is examined in relation to so-called difficult cases. Today it is standard for the patient and analyst together to analyse and understand the meaning of the ending, so that this can be found together. There is a beautiful quote by Wittgenstein (1931) in his ‘Notes on Frazer's Golden Bough’: ‘The awakening of the intellect takes place with the separation from the original soil, the original foundation of life’. So separation and separateness and the need to end the analysis awaken the mind. One can understand the start of every analysis containing the necessity for separation and the essentialness of the ending itself. ‘In the beginning is my end’, wrote T.S. Eliot. This is a description of the tension between resistance and transformation that the body of the analysis works through and at the end can achieve a new balance. For Winnicott, the aim of the psychoanalysis was to end it.
